Staples of Indian cooking.Ghee: Clarified butter with the milk solids cooked out, so it keeps for months without refrigeration. It is also valued in Ayurvedic tradition.
Staples of Indian cooking.Paneer: A fresh, unaged cheese made by curdling hot milk with acid. It doesn't melt, so it holds its shape in curries.
Staples of Indian cooking.Garam masala: The name means 'warming spice blend'. Recipes vary by family, but often include cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and cumin.
Staples of Indian cooking.Turmeric: Its curcumin pigment gives curries their golden color. India produces most of the world's turmeric, and the root is also used in rituals.
Staples of Indian cooking.Cumin: Cumin seeds are usually toasted in hot oil to start a dish, a step called tadka or tempering that releases their aroma.
Staples of Indian cooking.Cardamom: Called the 'queen of spices', it is among the world's priciest after saffron and vanilla. It scents both sweets and rice.
Staples of Indian cooking.Fenugreek: Its bitter seeds and dried leaves, kasuri methi, give many curries a maple-like aroma, and the same compound appears in artificial maple flavor.
Staples of Indian cooking.Asafoetida: Called hing, this pungent resin smells harsh raw but mellows into an onion-garlic flavor in hot oil. Some traditions use it instead of those.
Staples of Indian cooking.Curry leaves: These come from a tree and are fried whole at the start of South Indian dishes. They have nothing to do with curry powder.
Staples of Indian cooking.Tamarind: Sticky pods from a tropical tree give South Indian dishes a sweet-sour tang. Tamarind is also the base of Worcestershire sauce.
Staples of Indian cooking.Mustard seeds: They are fried until they pop, releasing nutty flavor. Bengali and South Indian cooking rely on them, and mustard oil is also common.
Staples of Indian cooking.Basmati rice: The name means 'fragrant', and the long grains lengthen rather than widen as they cook. Aged basmati is prized for its aroma.
Staples of Indian cooking.Jaggery: Unrefined cane or palm sugar, often dark and caramel-like. It's used in sweets and dals, and some regard it as more wholesome than white sugar.
Staples of Indian cooking.Miso: This fermented soybean paste is a Japanese cornerstone, made with a mold called koji and often aged for months.
Staples of Indian cooking.Nori: Japanese seaweed pressed into sheets, wrapping sushi. Nori has been farmed in Japan for centuries.
Staples of Indian cooking.Gochujang: A Korean paste of chili, glutinous rice and fermented soybeans. It is sweet, spicy and savory, and traditionally aged in earthen jars.
Staples of Indian cooking.Mirin: A sweet Japanese rice wine for cooking, whose sugars give teriyaki its glossy shine.
Staples of Indian cooking.Kombu: This dried kelp is the base of dashi and loaded with natural glutamate, the compound behind umami, first isolated from it in 1908.
Staples of Indian cooking.Mascarpone: A rich Italian cream cheese from Lombardy, and the heart of tiramisu. Italian cooks, not Indian ones, whip it into dessert.
Staples of Indian cooking.Parmesan: True Parmigiano Reggiano is aged at least 12 months in a few Italian provinces. It is Italian, not an Indian staple.
Staples of Indian cooking.Hoisin: Sweet, salty Chinese sauce of fermented soy with garlic and chilies. It's for Peking duck and Cantonese cooking, not Indian kitchens.
Staples of Indian cooking.Oyster sauce: A Cantonese condiment first made, according to legend, in 1888 when a cook accidentally left oysters simmering too long.
Staples of Indian cooking.Bonito flakes: Shaved smoked, dried skipjack tuna, a Japanese ingredient. The thin curls seem to dance on hot food.
Staples of Indian cooking.Maple syrup: It takes about 40 liters of sap to make one liter of syrup. North American, not Indian, in origin.

Animals that can regrow body parts.Starfish: A starfish can regrow a lost arm, and some species can regrow an entire body from a single arm.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Axolotl: Axolotls can regrow limbs, parts of the heart and even brain tissue, which makes them a research star.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Salamander: Salamanders regenerate limbs, tails and some organs, and their relatives the newts can even regrow eye lenses.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Gecko: Geckos can drop their tails to escape a predator, and a new one grows back, though usually shorter.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Flatworm: Flatworms called planarians can regenerate from tiny fragments, and each piece can become a complete worm.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Crab: Crabs can regrow lost claws over several moults, though the new claw is often smaller at first.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Lobster: Lobsters can regenerate lost claws and legs, and they keep growing throughout their lives.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Sea cucumber: Sea cucumbers can expel their internal organs when threatened and regrow them within weeks.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Zebrafish: Zebrafish can regenerate heart tissue, fins and spinal cord, and scientists study them for medical clues.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Octopus: Octopuses can regrow lost arms, and each arm has its own mini-brain of neurons.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Newt: Newts can regrow limbs, tails and even parts of the eye, retaining this ability for life.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Dog: Dogs can heal wounds but they can't regrow lost limbs or tails.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Cat: Cats can heal injuries but never regrow a lost limb or tail.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Elephant: Elephants can't regrow lost tusks, trunks or limbs.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Horse: Horses heal wounds but cannot regrow a lost limb or hoof.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Tiger: A tiger can't regrow a lost limb or claw, only heal the wound.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Parrot: Parrots can regrow feathers after moulting, but not lost toes or beaks.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Cow: Cows can't regenerate lost limbs, but their tough hide heals well.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Monkey: Monkeys cannot regrow a lost tail or limb, which stays missing.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Penguin: Penguins can't regrow lost flippers, though they replace all their feathers in an annual moult.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Snake: Snakes can't regrow a lost tail, though they shed their entire skin as they grow.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Kangaroo: Kangaroos cannot regrow a lost tail or limb, and the tail is a vital fifth leg for balance.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Tortoise: Tortoises cannot regrow a damaged shell, though minor cracks may slowly heal, because the shell is part of the skeleton.
Animals that can regrow body parts.Owl: Owls can't regrow lost talons or beak tissue, but they do replace their feathers each year.

Animals found in or around Antarctica.Emperor penguin: Emperor penguins breed in the dark Antarctic winter, with males balancing a single egg on their feet for about two months.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Adelie penguin: Adelie penguins build nests of pebbles, and males sometimes steal stones from their neighbours.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Leopard seal: Leopard seals are fierce hunters that eat penguins and even other seals, and they have a distinctive spotted coat.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Weddell seal: Weddell seals dive deeper than 600 metres and use their teeth to keep breathing holes open in the ice.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Krill: Antarctic krill are shrimp-like creatures that form some of the largest animal swarms on Earth, feeding whales, seals and penguins.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Orca: Orcas hunt in Antarctic waters, and some groups there specialise in washing seals off ice floes with waves.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Elephant seal: Elephant seals are the largest seals, with males weighing around four tonnes, and are named for the male's trunk-like nose.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Crabeater seal: The crabeater seal doesn't eat crabs; it strains krill through lace-like teeth and is among the most numerous large mammals on Earth.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Snow petrel: The snow petrel is a pure white seabird that breeds far inland on Antarctica, and it can spit stomach oil at intruders.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Skua: Skuas are aggressive seabirds that steal food and raid penguin colonies; they've been recorded even near the South Pole.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Polar bear: Polar bears live in the Arctic, at the opposite end of the Earth, and never meet penguins.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Walrus: Walruses live in Arctic waters, and none live around Antarctica.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Arctic fox: Arctic foxes live in the Arctic tundra, not in the Antarctic, where there are no land mammals.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Narwhal: Narwhals live in Arctic waters, far from Antarctica.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Beluga: Belugas are Arctic and sub-Arctic whales, and don't live near Antarctica.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Puffin: Puffins live in the northern Atlantic and Pacific, not in the southern polar region, where penguins fill their role.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Snowy owl: Snowy owls breed on the Arctic tundra, not in Antarctica.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Musk ox: Musk oxen live on the Arctic tundra, and Antarctica has no land mammals.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Reindeer: Reindeer live across the Arctic and subarctic, and Antarctica has no deer.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Lemming: Lemmings live in the Arctic tundra, which Antarctica lacks entirely; no rodents live there.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Moose: Moose live in northern forests of North America, Europe and Asia, not Antarctica.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Wolverine: Wolverines live in northern forests and tundra in the Northern Hemisphere, not around Antarctica.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Arctic hare: Arctic hares live in the far north and have no counterpart in Antarctica.
Animals found in or around Antarctica.Harp seal: Harp seals are born with white fur in the Arctic and don't live in Antarctica.

Ocean animals that are mammals.Whale: Whales are mammals that breathe air and nurse their young with milk. A blue whale calf drinks about 200 litres of milk daily.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Dolphin: Dolphins are mammals, and sleep with half the brain at a time. They identify each other with signature whistles, a kind of name.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Seal: Seals are marine mammals with blubber for warmth. A Weddell seal can hold its breath for around 80 minutes.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Sea lion: Sea lions are mammals, with ear flaps and strong front flippers. They're quick on land, and they can even rotate their back flippers to walk.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Walrus: Walruses are huge mammals with ivory tusks that can reach about a metre. They use the tusks to haul themselves onto the ice.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Manatee: Manatees are slow, plant-eating mammals. Their closest living relatives are elephants.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Dugong: The dugong is a marine mammal like the manatee, but with a whale-like fluked tail. It's thought to have inspired the mermaid legends.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Sea otter: Sea otters are mammals and have no blubber, only the densest fur of any animal. They use rocks as tools to crack shellfish.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Orca: Orcas, or killer whales, are in fact the largest dolphins. They live in family pods with distinct dialects, led by older females.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Narwhal: The narwhal is a whale whose long 'horn' is an overgrown tooth, a spiralled tusk. It's packed with nerve endings, and may sense the water.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Porpoise: Porpoises are small, shy cousins of dolphins, with spade-shaped teeth and no beak. The harbour porpoise is among the smallest cetaceans.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Polar bear: Polar bears are classified as marine mammals. They spend most of their lives on sea ice, and are strong swimmers.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Shark: Sharks are cartilaginous fish, with gills, not mammals. Their skeleton is cartilage, like your nose and ears.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Stingray: Stingrays are fish, flattened relatives of sharks. A few species have venomous spines in their tails.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Sea turtle: Sea turtles are reptiles, which lay eggs on beaches. They need to come up for air, but they're not mammals.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Penguin: Penguins are birds that cannot fly, but they swim superbly. They have feathers and lay eggs, like all birds.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Seahorse: Seahorses are bony fish that breathe through gills. Their upright swimming posture is unique among fish.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Octopus: Octopuses are molluscs with three hearts and blue blood. They're highly intelligent, but not remotely mammals.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Whale shark: The whale shark is a fish, not a whale, despite its size. It's the largest fish in the sea, and breathes with gills.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Eel: Eels are fish, snake-like, with gills. European eels travel thousands of kilometres to spawn in the Sargasso Sea.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Tuna: Tuna are fast, warm-bodied fish, but still fish. Bluefin tuna can reach speeds of about 70 km/h.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Swordfish: The swordfish is a fish with a long, flat bill. It can slash through schools of fish, and speeds past 80 km/h are claimed.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Sea snake: Sea snakes are reptiles, and most are highly venomous. They breathe air, and can stay under water for hours.
Ocean animals that are mammals.Marine iguana: The marine iguana of the Galápagos is the only sea-going lizard. It's a reptile, and sneezes out salt.

Cuts of beef.Sirloin: The legend of a king knighting a loin as 'Sir Loin' is false. The name comes from French surlonge, meaning above the loin.
Cuts of beef.Ribeye: Cut from the rib section, its marbling melts as it cooks, which gives it a rich flavor and tenderness.
Cuts of beef.Brisket: A chest cut full of connective tissue, which is why it needs hours of smoking or braising, as in Texas barbecue.
Cuts of beef.Flank: A lean, long cut from the belly muscles with strong grain, so slicing across the grain is the secret to tenderness.
Cuts of beef.T-bone: The T-shaped bone separates two cuts, the strip and a small piece of tenderloin.
Cuts of beef.Tenderloin: It comes from a muscle that barely works, so this is the most tender cut of beef, and also mild in flavor.
Cuts of beef.Chuck: From the shoulder, a hard-working muscle full of flavor and collagen; it's a favorite for burgers and pot roast.
Cuts of beef.Rump: From the hindquarter, this cut is a classic British steak that's more flavorful than tender.
Cuts of beef.Porterhouse: It's essentially a T-bone with a bigger tenderloin piece; the USDA requires the tenderloin to be at least 1.25 inches wide.
Cuts of beef.Skirt: It's a diaphragm muscle with beefy flavor, used for fajitas and Latin American arrachera.
Cuts of beef.Short rib: Cut across the bones in a thin strip, it becomes Korean galbi, grilled with sweet marinade.
Cuts of beef.Filet mignon: The French name means 'dainty fillet', which is cut from the tapering end of the tenderloin.
Cuts of beef.Tri-tip: A triangular cut from the bottom sirloin, famous in Santa Maria, California, barbecue.
Cuts of beef.Hanger: There is just one of these per animal, and it hangs from the diaphragm, which explains its old name 'butcher's steak'.
Cuts of beef.Pork belly: It's from a pig's underside, so it isn't beef, despite its bacon-like fat layers.
Cuts of beef.Ham: This is cured pig leg. Spain's jamón ibérico comes from acorn-fed pigs, not cows.
Cuts of beef.Prosciutto: Italian dry-cured ham, from pig. Parma ham is aged at least a year.
Cuts of beef.Bacon: Cured pork, famously breakfast, sold as strips; a pork product, not beef.
Cuts of beef.Drumstick: This is a poultry cut, from a chicken's or turkey's leg, not beef.
Cuts of beef.Pancetta: Italian cured pork belly. It's like bacon, but it isn't smoked, and it's pork.
Cuts of beef.Gammon: The British name for cured pork leg or back, a Christmas favorite. It's pork, not beef.
Cuts of beef.Rack of lamb: Cut from lamb, with rib bones frenched and clean. Lamb, not beef.
Cuts of beef.Pork chop: Cut from the pig, typically loin or rib. Pork, not beef.
Cuts of beef.Lamb shank: A shank is the lower leg of lamb that turns tender when slowly braised. Lamb, not beef.

Spanish islands.Majorca: The largest Balearic island. Chopin spent the winter of 1838 to 1839 in Valldemossa here, writing some of his preludes.
Spanish islands.Menorca: A UNESCO biosphere reserve. Some say mayonnaise was named after its capital Mahón, though the origin is debated.
Spanish islands.Ibiza: Founded by Phoenicians, its walled old town Dalt Vila is UNESCO-listed, long before it became famous for clubbing.
Spanish islands.Formentera: The smallest inhabited Balearic island, reachable only by sea, known for turquoise water and its lack of an airport.
Spanish islands.Tenerife: Teide, a volcano rising 3,715 metres, is the highest peak in Spain, and its observatory is famed for clear skies.
Spanish islands.Gran Canaria: Nicknamed a miniature continent because its dunes, forests and mountains give it very varied climates.
Spanish islands.Lanzarote: Volcanic eruptions in the 1730s reshaped much of this island, and artist César Manrique helped protect its look.
Spanish islands.Fuerteventura: It has the longest beaches in the Canaries, and strong steady winds make it a windsurfing and kitesurfing hot spot.
Spanish islands.La Palma: The 2021 Cumbre Vieja eruption lasted nearly three months and destroyed thousands of buildings. It also hosts major telescopes.
Spanish islands.La Gomera: Locals use Silbo Gomero, a whistled language that carries across deep ravines and is on UNESCO's heritage list.
Spanish islands.Madeira: A Portuguese island, famed for its fortified wine and flower festival, not Spanish.
Spanish islands.Azores: A Portuguese archipelago in the mid-Atlantic, where whale watching and volcanic crater lakes are the big draws.
Spanish islands.Corsica: A French island that is Napoleon's birthplace, closer to Italy than to mainland France.
Spanish islands.Sardinia: An Italian island with unusual long-lived residents and thousands of ancient stone towers called nuraghi.
Spanish islands.Sicily: The largest Mediterranean island, belonging to Italy, and home to Mount Etna, Europe's tallest active volcano.
Spanish islands.Malta: An independent country that is not Spanish, and its prehistoric temples are older than Stonehenge.
Spanish islands.Crete: Greece's largest island, where the Minoan civilization built palaces such as Knossos about 4,000 years ago.
Spanish islands.Rhodes: A Greek island once home to the Colossus, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
Spanish islands.Elba: An Italian island where Napoleon was exiled in 1814, before he escaped for his famous Hundred Days.
Spanish islands.Cape Verde: An independent island nation off West Africa, once a Portuguese colony, and not part of Spain.
Spanish islands.Porto Santo: A small Portuguese island near Madeira, known for its long golden beach, unlike Madeira's rocky shores.
Spanish islands.Capri: An Italian island in the Bay of Naples with its famous Blue Grotto, favoured by Roman emperors.
Spanish islands.Gozo: Malta's smaller sister island, with Ggantija temples that are among the oldest freestanding buildings in the world.
Spanish islands.Djerba: A Tunisian island with one of the oldest Jewish communities in the world, and not Spanish.

Languages of Africa.Swahili: A Bantu language with many Arabic loanwords that serves as the lingua franca across East Africa. "Safari" comes from it.
Languages of Africa.Amharic: Ethiopia's working language, written in the ancient Ge'ez script, which has hundreds of characters.
Languages of Africa.Yoruba: Spoken in Nigeria and Benin, it is tonal, and the famous talking drums imitate its speech patterns.
Languages of Africa.Zulu: South Africa's most widely spoken home language. Its word "ubuntu" expresses the idea that people are people through other people.
Languages of Africa.Hausa: A lingua franca of West Africa, spoken by tens of millions across Nigeria, Niger and beyond.
Languages of Africa.Igbo: One of Nigeria's three major languages and tonal. Chinua Achebe's novel Things Fall Apart is set in Igbo society.
Languages of Africa.Xhosa: Known for its click consonants, it was Nelson Mandela's mother tongue.
Languages of Africa.Somali: It became an officially written language only in 1972, using the Latin alphabet, after centuries as a mainly oral one.
Languages of Africa.Afrikaans: It evolved from Dutch in South Africa and is among the world's youngest standardised languages.
Languages of Africa.Wolof: Main language of Senegal's cities and of Dakar, spoken by many Gambians as well.
Languages of Africa.Tigrinya: Spoken in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, and written in the same Ge'ez script as Amharic.
Languages of Africa.Shona: The major language of Zimbabwe, associated with the great stone city of Great Zimbabwe and mbira thumb piano music.
Languages of Africa.Tagalog: The basis of Filipino, so a language of the Philippines and not Africa.
Languages of Africa.Quechua: The language of the Inca Empire, still spoken by millions in the Andes of South America.
Languages of Africa.Malay: It belongs to Southeast Asia, though the Malagasy language of Madagascar is a distant Austronesian relative.
Languages of Africa.Maori: The Polynesian language of New Zealand, with no African connection.
Languages of Africa.Thai: A tonal language of Thailand, spoken far from Africa.
Languages of Africa.Pashto: Spoken in Afghanistan and Pakistan, an Indo-Iranian language.
Languages of Africa.Hawaiian: A Polynesian language with only a few consonants and just 13 letters, from the Pacific.
Languages of Africa.Navajo: An Indigenous American language famous for code talkers in the Second World War, not African.
Languages of Africa.Basque: A European language isolate unrelated to any other living language, from Spain and France.
Languages of Africa.Gaelic: A Celtic language of Scotland and Ireland, spoken far from Africa.
Languages of Africa.Sami: Indigenous languages of the Arctic north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.
Languages of Africa.Inuktitut: An Indigenous language of Arctic Canada, written in syllabics, with no African link.

Cities that used to be national capitals.Rio de Janeiro: Brazil's capital until 1960, when the government moved inland to the purpose-built Brasília.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Bonn: West Germany's capital from 1949 until reunification, and the birthplace of Beethoven; Berlin took over in the 1990s.
Cities that used to be national capitals.St. Petersburg: Founded by Peter the Great in 1703, it served as Russia's imperial capital for two centuries until 1918, when the Bolsheviks moved to Moscow.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Istanbul: For centuries the Ottoman capital, as Constantinople before that, it lost the title to Ankara when Turkey became a republic in 1923.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Philadelphia: The US capital from 1790 to 1800 while Washington was being built, and where the Declaration of Independence was signed.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Melbourne: It hosted Australia's federal government from 1901 until 1927, while Canberra was constructed.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Almaty: Kazakhstan's largest city was the capital until 1997, when the government moved to the northern steppe city now called Astana.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Lagos: Nigeria's capital until 1991, when Abuja took over; it remains Africa's largest city by many counts.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Karachi: Pakistan's first capital after independence, until the new city of Islamabad was built in the 1960s.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Yangon: Myanmar's capital until 2005 to 2006, when the military government suddenly relocated to the new city of Naypyidaw.
Cities that used to be national capitals.New York City: The first US capital under the Constitution, where George Washington took his oath in 1789, before the government moved on in 1790.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Sydney: Sydney has never been the capital of Australia, though it was the seat of the colony of New South Wales and is the biggest city.
Cities that used to be national capitals.São Paulo: São Paulo is Brazil's largest city and economic engine, but it was never the national capital.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Cologne: Cologne is just north of Bonn, which was the West German capital, but Cologne itself never held that role.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Chicago: Chicago is a giant of the American Midwest but has never been a national capital.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Los Angeles: Los Angeles has never been the US capital, even though it's the center of its film industry.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Mumbai: Mumbai is India's financial capital, yet the national capital has been Delhi, and before 1911 Calcutta.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Liverpool: Liverpool is a great port, but England's capital has always been London.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Manchester: Manchester led the industrial revolution but has never been a national capital.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Marseille: Marseille is France's oldest city, founded by Greeks around 600 BCE, but the French capital has always been Paris.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Shanghai: Shanghai is China's largest city, but the Republic's capital in the 1920s and 1930s was Nanjing, and now it's Beijing.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Glasgow: Glasgow is Scotland's biggest city, but Edinburgh is the capital.
Cities that used to be national capitals.Dubai: Dubai is a major hub, yet the UAE's capital is Abu Dhabi, and Dubai has never been a national capital.

Chemical changes (not physical).Rusting: Iron combines with oxygen and water to form a brand-new compound, iron oxide, which is why rust crumbles and can't turn back.
Chemical changes (not physical).Burning wood: Combustion makes ash, CO2 and water vapor from the wood, and you can't un-burn a log, which marks a chemical change.
Chemical changes (not physical).Baking a cake: Heat triggers reactions among eggs, flour and baking soda, which make gas bubbles and a new texture you cannot reverse.
Chemical changes (not physical).Frying an egg: Heat permanently unravels the egg proteins, which then bond differently, so the white turns solid and opaque for good.
Chemical changes (not physical).Digestion: Enzymes and acids break food into new molecules your body can absorb; saliva starts the work on starch even before swallowing.
Chemical changes (not physical).Photosynthesis: Plants build sugar from CO2 and water using sunlight, and nearly all the oxygen we breathe came from it.
Chemical changes (not physical).Fermentation: Yeast turns sugar into alcohol and CO2 in making bread and beer, a reaction people have used for thousands of years.
Chemical changes (not physical).Tarnishing silver: Silver reacts with sulfur in the air to form dark silver sulfide, which is why polishing removes a layer.
Chemical changes (not physical).Fireworks exploding: The bursts and colors are combustion plus metal salts: strontium glows red, and copper gives blue.
Chemical changes (not physical).Milk souring: Bacteria turn lactose into lactic acid, giving the sour taste and curdling the proteins, and cheese and yogurt use this too.
Chemical changes (not physical).Toasting bread: Browning is the Maillard reaction between sugars and proteins, making new flavors that weren't in the bread.
Chemical changes (not physical).Rotting fruit: Microbes and enzymes break down the fruit into new compounds, which is why it smells and tastes different.
Chemical changes (not physical).Striking a match: Friction ignites chemicals in the head, and combustion makes new substances, light and heat.
Chemical changes (not physical).Melting ice: A trap: it's still H2O, just in liquid state, and refreezing brings the ice back, so it's a physical change.
Chemical changes (not physical).Boiling water: A trap: the steam is still H2O; cool it down and you get water again, so it is physical.
Chemical changes (not physical).Cutting paper: A trap: the pieces are smaller, but still paper, and nothing new is formed, so it's physical.
Chemical changes (not physical).Dissolving sugar: A trap: sugar vanishes into tea but is still sugar, and evaporating the water brings back the crystals.
Chemical changes (not physical).Crushing a can: A trap: it changes shape only; the aluminum is the same metal, so it's physical.
Chemical changes (not physical).Freezing juice: A trap: it turns solid, but no new substance forms, and thawing makes it juice again.
Chemical changes (not physical).Breaking glass: A trap: shards are still glass, and only the shape differs, which makes this a physical change.
Chemical changes (not physical).Tearing paper: A trap: the edges look different, but it is still paper, and no chemical bonds are formed anew.
Chemical changes (not physical).Evaporating puddle: A trap: liquid water becomes vapor, with the same H2O molecules, so it's a phase change, which is physical.
Chemical changes (not physical).Sharpening pencil: A trap: you remove wood and graphite shavings, but the materials don't change into anything else.
Chemical changes (not physical).Magnetizing a nail: A trap: the iron atoms' tiny magnetic regions line up, but the iron is still iron, so it is physical.

Units of volume.Liter: A cube 10 cm on each side holds exactly one liter, and so does 1,000 cubic centimeters; one liter of water weighs about one kilogram.
Units of volume.Gallon: A US gallon is about 3.79 liters, but a British imperial gallon is about 4.55, so the two countries don't agree.
Units of volume.Pint: A US pint is 16 fluid ounces while a British pint has 20, which is why pubs pour more beer in Britain.
Units of volume.Quart: Means a quarter of a gallon, which is where the name comes from, and it equals two pints.
Units of volume.Cup: A US cup is about 237 milliliters, but a metric cup is 250, which is a hidden source of recipe trouble.
Units of volume.Fluid ounce: Has a US and imperial version that differ slightly, and about 30 milliliters in the US.
Units of volume.Milliliter: One thousandth of a liter and the same as one cubic centimeter; a teaspoon holds about five.
Units of volume.Bushel: A dry volume for grain, about 35 liters in the US, and the word survives in the phrase a bushel and a peck.
Units of volume.Barrel: An oil barrel is 42 US gallons, a figure set in the 1860s Pennsylvania oil fields, and not like a beer barrel.
Units of volume.Tablespoon: About 15 milliliters in the US, or exactly three teaspoons, and it can be 20 ml in Australia.
Units of volume.Teaspoon: About five milliliters, and medicine labels use it, though real spoons from the kitchen vary quite a bit.
Units of volume.Cubic meter: The SI unit of volume, holding 1,000 liters; a cubic meter of water weighs about one tonne.
Units of volume.Cubic centimeter: Exactly one milliliter, and it's the cc you see in engine sizes, as in a 125cc motorbike.
Units of volume.Pound: A trap: a unit of weight or mass, not volume, although a pint of water weighs about a pound in some traditions.
Units of volume.Gram: A trap: measures mass; one gram is the mass of a milliliter of water, roughly.
Units of volume.Acre: A trap: a land area, not volume, defined traditionally as the land plowed in a day by oxen.
Units of volume.Hectare: A trap: a land area equal to 10,000 square meters, so it doesn't measure how much a container holds.
Units of volume.Meter: A trap: a length; only when cubed does it become a volume.
Units of volume.Mile: A trap: a length, about 1.6 kilometers, and not a volume.
Units of volume.Stone: A trap: a British weight of 14 pounds, so mass, not capacity.
Units of volume.Carat: A trap: a gem mass of 0.2 grams, not volume, so it measures how heavy a diamond is.
Units of volume.Ton: A trap: a unit of weight, though a shipping ton was once a volume, based on wine barrels called tuns.
Units of volume.Joule: A trap: a measure of energy, so not volume.
Units of volume.Kelvin: A trap: the SI temperature unit, starting at absolute zero, and not volume.

Radioactive substances.Uranium: The heaviest naturally abundant element, used for nuclear power. A single pellet the size of a fingertip holds as much energy as about a ton of coal.
Radioactive substances.Plutonium: Named after the dwarf planet Pluto, it is almost entirely man-made. It fueled the bomb dropped on Nagasaki.
Radioactive substances.Radium: Discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898. Factory workers once painted watch dials with glowing radium paint, with tragic health effects.
Radioactive substances.Radon: A colorless, odorless radioactive gas that seeps up from rock. Many countries recommend testing basements for it.
Radioactive substances.Polonium: Marie Curie named it after her native Poland. It's so intensely radioactive that it was used to poison Alexander Litvinenko in 2006.
Radioactive substances.Thorium: A weakly radioactive metal about as common as lead. Some think it could be a safer nuclear fuel than uranium.
Radioactive substances.Carbon-14: A radioactive form of carbon that decays at a known pace, with a half-life near 5,700 years. It lets scientists date ancient bones and wood.
Radioactive substances.Tritium: A radioactive form of hydrogen with two extra neutrons. It makes watch hands and exit signs glow without needing power.
Radioactive substances.Cesium-137: A radioactive by-product of nuclear fission with a half-life near 30 years. It was a central contaminant at Chernobyl and Fukushima.
Radioactive substances.Americium: Named for the Americas, it's in most household smoke detectors. A tiny speck ionizes air so the alarm can sense smoke.
Radioactive substances.Iodine-131: A radioactive iodine that collects in the thyroid. After nuclear accidents, people take ordinary iodine pills to block it.
Radioactive substances.Lead: A trap: lead is toxic but not radioactive. Lead is actually the stable end product of the decay of uranium.
Radioactive substances.Helium: A stable gas. Strangely, much helium on Earth comes from the radioactive decay of uranium and thorium underground.
Radioactive substances.Carbon-12: The common stable form of carbon, almost 99 percent of it. It defines the atomic mass unit, and is not radioactive.
Radioactive substances.Gold: A stable, nonradioactive element. All its atoms were forged in violent events like colliding neutron stars.
Radioactive substances.Iron: Stable and nonradioactive. Stars fuse atoms up to iron before they run out of energy, so it is the end of that chain.
Radioactive substances.Neon: A stable noble gas, so not radioactive, which fills glowing tubes. Its glow comes from electricity, not from any decay.
Radioactive substances.Mercury: Toxic but not radioactive. It was long used in thermometers, and its poison is chemical rather than from radiation.
Radioactive substances.Arsenic: A famous poison, but chemical rather than radioactive. It was nicknamed 'inheritance powder' for its use in murder mysteries.
Radioactive substances.Kryptonite: Fictional, the Superman-weakening rock of the comics. The real element krypton is an unreactive gas.
Radioactive substances.Titanium: A stable metal, not radioactive. It is strong and light, and it is also safe inside the body, so implants use it.
Radioactive substances.Cyanide: A fast-acting poison, but it works chemically, not through radiation. Some seeds, like apple pips, contain traces of it.
Radioactive substances.Asbestos: A mineral that causes lung disease from fibers, not radiation. It was long used as insulation because it doesn't burn.
Radioactive substances.Lithium: A stable light metal, not radioactive, used in batteries and in mood-stabilizing drugs. It is the lightest metal.

Medical imaging techniques.X-ray: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are blocked by dense bone, which is why fractures show up white on the film.
Medical imaging techniques.MRI: MRI uses strong magnets and radio waves, not radiation, to image soft tissue. The magnet is thousands of times stronger than a fridge magnet.
Medical imaging techniques.CT scan: A CT scan stitches many X-ray slices into a 3D picture. The name stands for computed tomography.
Medical imaging techniques.Ultrasound: Ultrasound uses sound far above human hearing. It is the safe way to see a baby before birth, with no radiation.
Medical imaging techniques.PET scan: A PET scan tracks a slightly radioactive sugar that builds up in busy tissue, so tumors and active brain areas glow.
Medical imaging techniques.Mammogram: A mammogram is a low-dose X-ray of the breast. It can spot tiny changes years before a lump could be felt.
Medical imaging techniques.Endoscopy: An endoscope is a thin flexible tube with a camera, letting doctors look inside the body through a natural opening.
Medical imaging techniques.Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is live X-ray video. Doctors use it to watch a swallowed contrast fluid move, or guide a catheter in real time.
Medical imaging techniques.Angiogram: An angiogram uses X-rays and a contrast dye to make blood vessels visible, often to find blockages near the heart.
Medical imaging techniques.Echocardiogram: An echocardiogram is an ultrasound of the heart, showing its valves and chambers moving in real time.
Medical imaging techniques.Blood test: A blood test analyses a sample in a lab. It gives data, but no picture of the body's insides.
Medical imaging techniques.Biopsy: A biopsy takes a tissue sample, which is then examined under a microscope. It is the way to confirm cancer, but it's not imaging.
Medical imaging techniques.ECG: An ECG records the heart's electrical signals as a line trace. It is a graph of activity, not a picture of structure.
Medical imaging techniques.Stethoscope: A stethoscope is for listening. It was invented in 1816 by Laennec, who rolled paper to avoid pressing his ear on a patient.
Medical imaging techniques.Urinalysis: Urinalysis checks urine for signs of illness. It is chemistry and microscopy, not imaging.
Medical imaging techniques.Thermometer: A thermometer gives one number, your temperature. It cannot show anything inside you.
Medical imaging techniques.Reflex hammer: A reflex hammer tests nerve reflexes by tapping the tendon. It checks function but creates no images.
Medical imaging techniques.Blood pressure cuff: A blood pressure cuff measures pressure in the arteries in mmHg. It is a measurement, not an image.
Medical imaging techniques.Vaccine: A vaccine trains the immune system. It is a treatment, not a diagnostic imaging method.
Medical imaging techniques.Defibrillator: A defibrillator shocks a stopped or quivering heart back into rhythm. It treats, but it makes no picture of the body.
Medical imaging techniques.Pulse oximeter: A pulse oximeter clips onto a finger and uses red light to estimate blood oxygen; a number, not a picture.
Medical imaging techniques.Allergy test: An allergy test pricks the skin with small amounts of allergens. It looks for a reaction, not at an image.
Medical imaging techniques.Throat swab: A throat swab collects cells for a lab test, such as strep or COVID. It identifies germs, not pictures of tissue.
Medical imaging techniques.EEG: An EEG records the brain's electrical waves from scalp electrodes. It's a trace of activity, not an image of structure.

Involuntary body actions.Heartbeat: Your heart beats on its own, thanks to pacemaker cells, and a transplanted heart will keep beating without any nerve connection.
Involuntary body actions.Digestion: Digestion runs without any thought, and your gut muscles squeeze food along in waves called peristalsis, even while you sleep.
Involuntary body actions.Sweating: Sweating is automatic: a rise in body heat triggers about two to four million sweat glands. Cooling happens as it evaporates.
Involuntary body actions.Goosebumps: Goosebumps are a leftover of ancestors with more fur. Tiny muscles pull each hair up to trap warmth or look bigger.
Involuntary body actions.Shivering: Shivering is the body producing heat by rapid muscle twitches, and you can't turn it off at will.
Involuntary body actions.Hiccups: Hiccups are sudden spasms of the diaphragm followed by the vocal cords snapping shut. Their purpose is still a mystery.
Involuntary body actions.Sneezing: A sneeze is a reflex that can send droplets out at tens of miles per hour, and it is hard to stop once it starts.
Involuntary body actions.Knee-jerk reflex: The doctor's hammer test works because the reflex arc goes through the spinal cord and skips the brain entirely.
Involuntary body actions.Pupil dilation: Your pupils widen in the dark and shrink in bright light on their own, and also widen with strong emotion or interest.
Involuntary body actions.Blushing: Blushing is the face's blood vessels widening from embarrassment. Even Darwin called it the most human of expressions.
Involuntary body actions.Gag reflex: The gag reflex protects the airway from choking. It can be triggered by touch alone and varies a lot between people.
Involuntary body actions.Walking: Walking is voluntary, even though it feels automatic. You choose to start, stop and steer.
Involuntary body actions.Talking: Talking is voluntary: it uses dozens of muscles, but you choose what to say, which sets it apart from reflexes.
Involuntary body actions.Writing: Writing is a learned, voluntary skill. You choose each stroke, unlike a reflex, which happens without thinking.
Involuntary body actions.Whistling: Whistling is a deliberate act: you choose to shape your lips and control your breath.
Involuntary body actions.Chewing gum: Chewing is voluntary, which is why you can stop mid-bite, though once started it can feel automatic.
Involuntary body actions.Waving: Waving is a deliberate gesture you choose to make, so it is voluntary, unlike a reflex that happens automatically.
Involuntary body actions.Clapping: Clapping is voluntary, though crowds sometimes start it almost automatically. Still, every clap is a muscle choice.
Involuntary body actions.Jumping: Jumping is voluntary, though a sudden loud noise can trigger a startle reflex that makes you jump without choosing.
Involuntary body actions.Winking: Winking is voluntary, and it differs from a blink, which is a reflex. That is why winking takes conscious effort.
Involuntary body actions.Reading: Reading is a learned, conscious activity, though your eyes still jump in tiny steps called saccades without your control.
Involuntary body actions.Singing: Singing is voluntary, though it uses involuntary breathing muscles too, which you can choose to control.
Involuntary body actions.Typing: Typing is a voluntary skill. Experts type so fast it feels automatic, but it is still planned movement.
Involuntary body actions.Kicking: Kicking is a voluntary movement. The knee-jerk reflex is different, since doctors can trigger it with a tap.

Names for note lengths.Whole note: In the US it is the whole note, and it lasts four beats in common time.
Names for note lengths.Half note: Lasts two beats in common time, drawn with a hollow notehead and a stem.
Names for note lengths.Quarter note: The one-beat note in common time, the note most songs count along to.
Names for note lengths.Eighth note: Half a beat in common time, with a flag, and pairs are often joined by a beam.
Names for note lengths.Sixteenth note: Two flags or beams, lasting a quarter of a beat in common time.
Names for note lengths.Crotchet: British name for the quarter note. It comes from the French for a little hook, from the note's shape.
Names for note lengths.Quaver: The British eighth note. The word shares a root with the old verb to quaver, meaning to tremble.
Names for note lengths.Minim: The British half note, from the Latin for smallest. In medieval music it was the shortest note around.
Names for note lengths.Semibreve: The British whole note, literally half a breve. The breve is twice as long, so it is the longest note in common use.
Names for note lengths.Semiquaver: The British sixteenth note, with two tails, which gives it a quick, fluttering sound.
Names for note lengths.Demisemiquaver: A 32nd note, with three flags. One of the longest music terms for one of the shortest regular notes.
Names for note lengths.Treble clef: The curly symbol at the start of the staff comes from a decorated letter G and curls around the G line.
Names for note lengths.Bass clef: It descends from a stylised letter F, and its two dots sit either side of the F line.
Names for note lengths.Sharp: Raises a note by a half-step, so it changes pitch, not length.
Names for note lengths.Flat: Lowers a note by a half-step, and its shape comes from a rounded letter b.
Names for note lengths.Natural: Cancels a sharp or flat, so the note returns to its plain form. It changes pitch, not length.
Names for note lengths.Fermata: The Italian word means pause, and the player holds the note longer than written. A bird's-eye shape hangs above it.
Names for note lengths.Time signature: It says how many beats are in a bar and which note gets one beat, but it does not name a note length.
Names for note lengths.Bar line: The vertical line divides music into measures, so it names no length.
Names for note lengths.Staff: Five lines and four spaces hold the notes, and it is not a note.
Names for note lengths.Tie: A tie joins two notes of the same pitch so you hold their combined length. A trap, because it affects length but names nothing.
Names for note lengths.Slur: A slur looks like a tie but joins different notes, telling you to play them smoothly. It does not name a duration.
Names for note lengths.Key signature: Sharps or flats at the start of the staff tell you the key, and they name no note length.
Names for note lengths.Coda: Italian for tail, it marks the closing section of a piece, so it is a place, not a length.

Girl groups.The Bangles: They topped the 1986 US chart with Walk Like an Egyptian, and Eternal Flame hit number one in 1989.
Girl groups.Fifth Harmony: They formed on The X Factor US in 2012, and Worth It was a hit with a Latin pop flair.

Girl groups.Blackpink: In 2023 they became the first Korean group to headline Coachella, helping K-pop reach new heights.
Girl groups.The Ronettes: Ronnie Spector fronted them, and Be My Baby was produced by her husband Phil Spector with his Wall of Sound.
Girl groups.Backstreet Boys: A boy band from Orlando, famous for I Want It That Way, not a girl group.
Girl groups.One Direction: A boy band formed on The X Factor in 2010, with Harry Styles among its members.
Girl groups.Take That: A British boy band with Gary Barlow, with Back for Good a big hit.
Girl groups.BTS: A Korean boy band, whose fan base is called the ARMY.

Girl groups.Fleetwood Mac: A mixed band of men and women, led partly by Stevie Nicks, famed for Rumours.
