Girl groups.The Carpenters: A brother and sister duo, famous for Close to You, so not a girl group.
Girl groups.Westlife: An Irish boy band with 14 UK number-ones.
Girl groups.Roxette: A Swedish duo of one woman and one man, famous for The Look and It Must Have Been Love.
Girl groups.Eurythmics: A duo of Annie Lennox and Dave Stewart, famed for Sweet Dreams.
Girl groups.Boyz II Men: A boy band with New Jack Swing and gospel harmonies, whose End of the Road topped the chart.

Soccer terms.Offside: Offside catches an attacker nearer the goal than the ball and the second-last defender; the rule dates back to 1863 and is now checked by VAR.
Soccer terms.Penalty kick: A penalty kick is taken from 12 yards, and goalkeepers save roughly one in four.
Soccer terms.Corner kick: A corner kick restarts play after the defense puts the ball behind its own goal line, and a goal can be scored directly from one, called an Olimpico.
Soccer terms.Header: A header uses the forehead, and research on brain health has led to limits on heading in youth soccer in some countries.
Soccer terms.Throw-in: A throw-in restarts play from the sideline, and must be taken with both hands and both feet on the ground.
Soccer terms.Yellow card: Ken Aston, an English referee, got the idea from a traffic light in 1966, and cards debuted at the 1970 World Cup.
Soccer terms.Red card: A red card sends a player off, and the team continues short-handed without a replacement.
Soccer terms.Free kick: A free kick is awarded for fouls, and the defenders must stand at least 10 yards from the ball, which is why they form a wall.
Soccer terms.Nutmeg: A nutmeg is passing the ball between an opponent's legs, which is considered an insult by many players.
Soccer terms.Bicycle kick: A bicycle kick sends the ball backward over the kicker's head; Pelé helped popularize it, and Cristiano Ronaldo's 2018 one for Real Madrid is a classic.
Soccer terms.Stoppage time: Stoppage time adds minutes to account for delays, and the referee's figure is the minimum, since play can run beyond it.
Soccer terms.Own goal: An own goal is scored by a defender into his own net, and it's credited to the opposing team.
Soccer terms.Touchdown: A touchdown is American football's, and in soccer you cannot score by carrying the ball over a line.
Soccer terms.Home run: A home run is baseball's; soccer's thrill is the long-range screamer.
Soccer terms.Wicket: A wicket is cricket's three stumps; a soccer goal is 8 yards wide and 8 feet high, and its crossbar has stopped many shots.
Soccer terms.Puck: A puck is hockey's flat rubber disc; a soccer ball is a sphere about 22 centimeters across, traditionally stitched from 32 panels.
Soccer terms.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is basketball's; soccer outlaws the use of hands in play except for the goalkeeper.
Soccer terms.Bunt: A bunt is baseball's soft hit, and in soccer the quiet pass is called a chip or a through ball.
Soccer terms.Birdie: A birdie is golf's; soccer's bird mascots include Crystal Palace's eagle and Newcastle's magpies.
Soccer terms.Scrum: A scrum is rugby's; in soccer the contest for a loose ball is a tackle or challenge.
Soccer terms.Lineout: A lineout is rugby's restart with a lifted jumper; soccer's sideline restart is the plain throw-in.
Soccer terms.Icing: Icing is hockey's rule about shooting the puck the length of the rink; no soccer rule exists like it.
Soccer terms.Ace: An ace is tennis's unreturnable serve; soccer's nearest thing is a goal from a corner or direct free kick.
Soccer terms.Googly: A googly is cricket's; a soccer deceiver is a dummy or a step-over.

Triathlon gear.Wetsuit: Neoprene adds buoyancy and warmth, and swimmers can be several seconds per 100 meters faster. Races ban them in warm water, over a set temperature.
Triathlon gear.Bicycle: The longest leg of most triathlons is on two wheels. Triathlon bikes use aerodynamic frames with a steeper seat angle than road bikes.
Triathlon gear.Running shoes: Triathletes often fit them with elastic laces so they slip on quickly. Saving a few seconds in transition can decide a close race.
Triathlon gear.Goggles: They keep water out of the eyes and help a swimmer sight buoys. Many triathletes pick tinted lenses for glare from open-water sunlight.
Triathlon gear.Swim cap: Colored caps help officials tell age groups apart. They also reduce drag and keep hair out of the eyes.
Triathlon gear.Helmet: Required in every triathlon, the helmet must be buckled before you touch the bike. Time-trial helmets with long tails can reduce aerodynamic drag.
Triathlon gear.Race belt: A stretchy belt that holds the bib number. It saves precious seconds because it can be flipped around for the run instead of pinned on.
Triathlon gear.Bike shoes: Stiff-soled shoes that clip into the pedals. Many triathletes leave them clipped on the bike and slip in while rolling, saving time.
Triathlon gear.Tri suit: A one-piece suit worn for all three legs. It dries fast and has a thin pad for the bike, so no one must change clothes.
Triathlon gear.Energy gel: A sweet packet of quick carbohydrates carried for long bike and run legs. It tastes strong but can prevent hitting the wall.
Triathlon gear.Water bottle: Triathletes mount bottles on the frame or between aero bars. Hydration matters most on the bike, where it is easiest to drink.
Triathlon gear.Skis: Equipment for snow sports. Winter triathlon exists, but it swaps in running, mountain biking and cross-country skiing instead of swimming.
Triathlon gear.Racket: Used in tennis, squash and badminton. The triathlon is a three-discipline race, so no one hits anything.
Triathlon gear.Puck: The hard rubber disc in ice hockey. Triathlon is not a stick sport, and no puck ever needs to be chased.
Triathlon gear.Oar: Used in rowing, which is not part of triathlon. The swim is done without any equipment other than goggles and maybe a wetsuit.
Triathlon gear.Paddle: Used in canoeing and kayaking. Triathletes swim without paddles, though some training aids called hand paddles exist for practice.
Triathlon gear.Snorkel: Triathletes can use one only in training. In races, officials ban it, as it gives a swimmer an unfair breathing edge.
Triathlon gear.Kayak: A paddled boat that has no place in triathlon. Its cousin, the paddle leg, appears in some multisport events such as the Coast to Coast race in New Zealand.
Triathlon gear.Ice skates: Blades for gliding on ice. A triathlon is on land and open water, so a skate would have no use.
Triathlon gear.Javelin: A spear thrown in track and field. Triathlon is a pure endurance event, so throwing is not a part of it.
Triathlon gear.Golf club: Sports gear for hitting a ball far. Triathletes aim for stamina, and they never carry one during a race.
Triathlon gear.Ice axe: A mountaineering tool for steep ice. Triathlon courses are flat, paved and open-water, so one would only slow you down.
Triathlon gear.Surfboard: A board for riding waves. Triathletes swim, not surf, though open-water starts can be as rough as a beach break.
Triathlon gear.Flippers: Fins are banned in standard triathlon swims. They make a swimmer much faster, which would defeat the point of the race.

Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Odysseus: The king of Ithaca took ten years to get home from Troy, and also conceived the Trojan Horse trick.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Penelope: Odysseus's wife held off suitors for years by weaving a shroud by day and secretly unraveling it by night.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Oedipus: He solved the Sphinx's riddle, then unknowingly fulfilled a prophecy by killing his father and marrying his mother.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Jason: He led the Argonauts to Colchis for the Golden Fleece, helped by the sorceress Medea.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Icarus: He flew with wax-and-feather wings made by his father; the wax melted when he rose too near the sun.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Daedalus: Master craftsman who built the Labyrinth on Crete, then escaped it with wings; his name is a byword for ingenuity.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).King Midas: Dionysus granted his wish that everything he touched turn to gold, which nearly starved him, until he washed in the river Pactolus.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Pandora: Often called the first woman; her 'box' was actually a large jar (pithos) in the original Greek.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Theseus: The Athenian hero who killed the Minotaur and is said to have unified Attica; his ship was kept for centuries as a philosophy puzzle.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Achilles: A mortal despite a sea-goddess mother, Thetis; Homer's 'Iliad' never mentions the famous heel story.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Agamemnon: King of Mycenae and leader of the Greeks at Troy, murdered by his wife Clytemnestra on his return.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Zeus: A trap: the king of the gods is no mortal, though he fathered many mortal heroes.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Hera: A trap: Zeus's wife and sister is a goddess, not a mortal, queen of the Olympians.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Athena: A trap: goddess of wisdom who sprang from Zeus's head, never mortal.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Apollo: Olympian god of music and the sun, though he serves mortal Admetus for a year as punishment.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Hermes: A trap: messenger of the gods, who guides souls to the underworld, never mortal.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Hades: A trap: lord of the underworld, and thus a god, not mortal, whose realm bears his name.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Persephone: A trap: she's the daughter of Demeter and queen of the underworld, and a goddess, even though she was abducted.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Dionysus: A trap: his mother Semele was mortal, yet he is a full god, the only Olympian with a mortal parent to join the twelve.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Eros: God of love, whose arrows made gods and mortals fall for someone; the Romans called him Cupid.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Nike: Goddess of victory, and the namesake of the sportswear brand, whose swoosh evokes her wing.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Nemesis: A trap: the goddess of retribution, who punished arrogance, was a god rather than a mortal.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Helios: A trap: the sun's Titan god drives his chariot across the sky daily, no mortal.
Mortals of Greek myth (not gods).Gaia: The primordial Earth goddess, mother of Titans; her name lives on in 'geology' and 'geography'.

Russian monarchs.Peter the Great: Tsar from 1682 and emperor from 1721, who founded St Petersburg and once worked as a shipwright abroad. He taxed beards to push modernity.
Russian monarchs.Ivan the Terrible: The first to be crowned Tsar of all Russia, in 1547. St Basil's Cathedral was built on his order, and his later years brought paranoia and brutal purges.
Russian monarchs.Catherine the Great: German-born, she took power in 1762 after a coup against her husband Peter III. She expanded Russia southward and corresponded with Voltaire.
Russian monarchs.Nicholas II: Russia's last tsar, who abdicated in 1917 and was executed with his family in 1918. His son Alexei had haemophilia.
Russian monarchs.Alexander II: The "Tsar Liberator" who freed the serfs in 1861. Assassinated in 1881 by a bomb, he was killed on the day he considered a constitutional reform.
Russian monarchs.Alexander I: Tsar during Napoleon's 1812 invasion, who later entered Paris with his army in 1814. Some tales say he faked his death to become a hermit.
Russian monarchs.Nicholas I: Tsar 1825 to 1855, remembered as a stern autocrat. He died during the Crimean War, which Russia was losing.
Russian monarchs.Boris Godunov: Elected tsar in 1598 after Ivan's dynasty ended. Pushkin and Mussorgsky both turned his story into art, and his reign preceded the Time of Troubles.
Russian monarchs.Paul I: Tsar from 1796 to 1801, who was murdered by conspirators in his palace. He is known for a strict military approach.
Russian monarchs.Alexander III: Tsar from 1881 to 1894, a huge man said to bend iron by hand. He commissioned Fabergé eggs, a tradition his son continued.
Russian monarchs.Rasputin: A mystic peasant who gained influence over the last tsar's family by seeming to ease Alexei's illness. He was murdered in 1916 but never ruled.
Russian monarchs.Lenin: Led the Bolshevik revolution in 1917 and headed the Soviet state. He overthrew the monarchy, not ruled as monarch.
Russian monarchs.Stalin: Soviet leader from the 1920s until 1953, a dictator but not a monarch. Born Ioseb Jughashvili in Georgia.
Russian monarchs.Trotsky: A Bolshevik leader who built the Red Army. He lost to Stalin, was exiled, and was killed in Mexico in 1940 with an ice axe.
Russian monarchs.Tolstoy: The author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina, a Russian count. He wrote of kings, but never ruled.
Russian monarchs.Pushkin: Russia's national poet, who died in a duel in 1837 at 37. He was a writer, not a monarch.
Russian monarchs.Wilhelm II: The German emperor and cousin of Nicholas II, with whom he exchanged "Willy-Nicky" letters. He was German, not Russian.
Russian monarchs.Louis XVI: King of France guillotined in 1793. French, not Russian, and an absolute monarch in his own right.
Russian monarchs.Frederick the Great: The Prussian king who admired French culture. He fought Russia in the Seven Years' War, but he was no Russian ruler.
Russian monarchs.Napoleon: Invaded Russia in 1812 and lost most of his Grande Armée. He was a French emperor.
Russian monarchs.Tchaikovsky: The composer of Swan Lake and the Nutcracker. He was Russian, but he was no monarch.
Russian monarchs.Ivan Pavlov: The Russian physiologist whose dogs salivated at a bell, inspiring the idea of conditioned reflexes. He won the 1904 Nobel Prize.
Russian monarchs.Dostoevsky: The Russian novelist of Crime and Punishment, who survived a mock execution in 1849. He was a writer, not a ruler.
Russian monarchs.Anastasia: The tsar's youngest daughter, executed in 1918. Impostor Anna Anderson claimed to be her, but DNA tests disproved it. She was a grand duchess, never a ruler.

Things you can plug into a USB port.Mouse: Most mice draw so little power that USB can run them directly, no battery needed, and the standard supplies 5 volts.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Keyboard: USB keyboards report up to six keys pressed at once in basic mode, which is why some cheap ones ghost on many keys.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Flash drive: The first USB flash drives arrived around 2000 and held just 8 megabytes; today they hold terabytes.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Webcam: The first webcam watched a coffee pot at Cambridge University in 1991 so researchers could see if it was empty.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Printer: Printers often connect over USB-B, the squarish plug that is a relic of the standard's early years.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Headphones: USB headphones carry a tiny sound card inside the cable, so the conversion happens before the signal reaches your ears.
Things you can plug into a USB port.External hard drive: Portable hard drives get all their power from the USB port, and a spinning one can hit a limit on weak ports.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Game controller: Many controllers plug in over USB for charging and a lag-free link, which is why competitive players prefer them wired.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Microphone: USB microphones contain their own converter, so podcasters can record straight to a computer with no mixer.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Phone cable: Phone cables use USB-C now, and the plug is reversible, so you never have to guess which way it goes in.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Card reader: A card reader lets a computer read camera SD cards, and each tiny card stores a lot of photos.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Scanner: Flatbed scanners can run on USB power alone, and a lamp moves slowly under the glass as it captures the image.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Toaster: A toaster draws well over a thousand watts, and USB supplies only a few watts, so it needs the wall socket.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Kettle: A kettle needs about 2,000 watts to boil water quickly; USB is roughly a hundred times too weak.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Hair dryer: Hair dryers pull 1,200 watts or more, far past anything a USB port could deliver.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Fridge: A fridge needs mains power for its compressor, and it is far too hungry for a USB cable.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Stapler: A stapler is a manual tool, so it needs no power at all, though electric ones plug into the wall.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Blender: A blender motor pulls hundreds of watts, and USB blenders exist only as small personal cups.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Clothes iron: An iron needs about 1,000 watts of heat, and no USB port can give it that.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Microwave: A microwave oven draws over a thousand watts to generate its waves, so it plugs into the wall.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Dishwasher: A dishwasher heats water and runs pumps, so it is hardwired to the home's electrical system.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Washing machine: A washing machine uses mains power to heat and spin heavy loads, and USB could not move a drum.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Ceiling fan: Ceiling fans are wired into the house circuit, though small USB desk fans are very popular.
Things you can plug into a USB port.Lawnmower: A mower needs a big battery or an engine, and a USB plug gives only a trickle of power.

Rooms in a house.Kitchen: Kitchens became the heart of the home only in the 1900s; before that, many were hot, smoky rooms kept far from the dining area.
Rooms in a house.Bathroom: Indoor plumbing was a luxury until the late 1800s, and the bathroom did not become standard in homes until the 20th century.
Rooms in a house.Bedroom: People once slept in the main hall, and private bedrooms spread through ordinary homes only in the last few hundred years.
Rooms in a house.Living room: The living room took its name in the early 1900s; before it was the parlor, a stiff room kept for guests.
Rooms in a house.Dining room: Formal dining rooms became popular in Victorian times, and many modern homes have dropped them for open-plan kitchens.
Rooms in a house.Attic: The word attic comes from Attica, the region of Athens, and refers to a Greek style of low decorative story under a roof.
Rooms in a house.Basement: Basements keep a steady cool temperature year round because the ground around them barely changes, which is why they suit wine.
Rooms in a house.Pantry: Pantry comes from the Latin word for bread, panis, because it was where the loaves were stored.
Rooms in a house.Laundry room: Laundry rooms are often near the kitchen or bedrooms, and the washer and dryer became standard household items after World War II.
Rooms in a house.Study: A study is a room for reading or work, a quiet space that grew from the Renaissance idea of a private studiolo.
Rooms in a house.Nursery: Nurseries were once on upper floors far from adult spaces, and their name goes back to the word for nurse.
Rooms in a house.Conservatory: Conservatories were glass rooms built to protect tender plants, such as orange trees, over the cold winters.
Rooms in a house.Den: A den is a cozy room for relaxing, and the word comes from a wild animal's lair.
Rooms in a house.Driveway: A driveway is outside, not a room; the word first meant a drive through grounds toward a house.
Rooms in a house.Patio: A patio is an outdoor paved area, and the word comes from Spanish for a courtyard.
Rooms in a house.Lawn: A lawn is outside, and the word probably comes from the French launde, meaning a glade.
Rooms in a house.Chimney: A chimney is a structure that carries smoke upward, a part of a house but not a room.
Rooms in a house.Roof: A roof is a covering, not a room, though attics make rooms out of the space below it.
Rooms in a house.Gutter: A gutter collects rain at the edge of a roof and carries it away, and is not a room.
Rooms in a house.Fence: A fence marks a boundary around a yard, and is outside the house walls.
Rooms in a house.Mailbox: A mailbox is a tiny box at the roadside, not a room, and the US ones are regulated by the postal service.
Rooms in a house.Garden: A garden is outdoors, though a conservatory brings it halfway inside.
Rooms in a house.Doorstep: A doorstep is the step by the front door and is just outside the house, not a room.
Rooms in a house.Sidewalk: A sidewalk is a public path beside the road, and it belongs to the town, not to the house.

Things you'd use in the shower.Shampoo: Modern shampoo is a detergent that lifts oil and dirt, and the first bottled shampoo sold in the 1900s.
Things you'd use in the shower.Conditioner: Conditioner coats hair with positively charged ingredients that smooth the cuticle, which tames tangles and frizz.
Things you'd use in the shower.Body wash: Body wash is a liquid cleanser, and it has been gaining on bar soap for decades.
Things you'd use in the shower.Loofah: A loofah is not a sea sponge but the dried fibrous interior of a gourd, the Luffa plant.
Things you'd use in the shower.Bar of soap: Soap-making dates back thousands of years, and a bar is made by reacting fats with an alkali.
Things you'd use in the shower.Shower cap: A shower cap keeps your hair dry, and it is also handy for covering shoes in a packed suitcase.
Things you'd use in the shower.Washcloth: A washcloth is a small terry square, and it gives gentle exfoliation while you wash.
Things you'd use in the shower.Body scrub: Body scrubs use salt, sugar or tiny beads to slough away dead skin, but microbeads have been banned in many places.
Things you'd use in the shower.Pumice stone: Pumice is volcanic rock so full of gas bubbles that it can actually float on water.
Things you'd use in the shower.Back brush: A long-handled back brush reaches the spots your hands cannot.
Things you'd use in the shower.Face wash: Face washes are formulated more gently than body soap because facial skin is thinner and more sensitive.
Things you'd use in the shower.Hair dryer: A hair dryer is electric, and using one in the shower would be dangerous.
Things you'd use in the shower.Deodorant: Deodorant goes on after the shower, since it works best on clean, dry skin.
Things you'd use in the shower.Hairspray: Hairspray is applied after styling, since water would wash it right out.
Things you'd use in the shower.Makeup brush: Makeup is applied after you are clean and dry, and not in the shower.
Things you'd use in the shower.Lipstick: Lipstick goes on at the mirror, since it would just wash off in a shower.
Things you'd use in the shower.Perfume: Perfume is applied after drying off, since steam and water would waste it.
Things you'd use in the shower.Nail polish: Nail polish is applied on dry nails, and water would ruin the finish.
Things you'd use in the shower.Sunglasses: Sunglasses are for sun, not shower; steam would fog them completely.
Things you'd use in the shower.Hair straightener: A hair straightener heats up to roughly 180 degrees Celsius and must never meet water.
Things you'd use in the shower.Talcum powder: Talc is a mineral that absorbs moisture, so it belongs with dry skin after the shower.
Things you'd use in the shower.Lint roller: A lint roller works on dry clothes, and a shower would ruin its sticky sheet.
Things you'd use in the shower.Curling iron: A curling iron is electric and heated, and it can not be taken into the shower.
Things you'd use in the shower.Hand cream: Hand cream is applied after washing, and in the shower it would just rinse off.

Human bones by their everyday names.Collarbone: The collarbone, or clavicle, is the most commonly broken bone in the body and the only long bone that lies horizontally.
Human bones by their everyday names.Kneecap: The kneecap, or patella, is a floating bone that sits in a tendon and shields the knee joint.
Human bones by their everyday names.Shinbone: The shinbone, or tibia, is the second-longest bone in the body, and you can feel it right under the skin.
Human bones by their everyday names.Thighbone: The thighbone, or femur, is the longest and strongest bone in the body, about a quarter of your height.
Human bones by their everyday names.Breastbone: The breastbone, or sternum, is a flat bone in the middle of the chest, and it's where the ribs join in front.
Human bones by their everyday names.Tailbone: The tailbone, or coccyx, is a leftover of the tail our distant ancestors had, and it still anchors some muscles.
Human bones by their everyday names.Cheekbone: The cheekbone, or zygomatic bone, shapes the face and forms part of the eye socket.
Human bones by their everyday names.Jawbone: The jawbone, or mandible, is the only skull bone that moves, and it's the strongest bone in the face.
Human bones by their everyday names.Shoulder blade: The shoulder blade, or scapula, is a flat triangular bone that glides over the back of your ribs.
Human bones by their everyday names.Hipbone: The hipbone is actually three fused bones, the ilium, ischium and pubis, and it makes up part of the pelvis.
Human bones by their everyday names.Rib: Humans have 24 ribs in 12 pairs, and they protect the heart and lungs while flexing as you breathe.
Human bones by their everyday names.Anklebone: The anklebone is the talus, which sits between the shin and the heel bone, and passes all your weight to the foot.
Human bones by their everyday names.Funny bone: The funny bone is not a bone at all: it's the ulnar nerve running past your elbow, and the pun is on humerus.
Human bones by their everyday names.Wishbone: A wishbone is a bird's fused collarbone, the furcula, and tradition says the one who gets the bigger half gets the wish.
Human bones by their everyday names.T-bone: A T-bone is a steak with a T-shaped bone, which is a cut from the vertebra of a cow, and it's not human.
Human bones by their everyday names.Trombone: A trombone is a brass instrument with a slide. The 'bone' in it is just part of the name, which comes from Italian for large trumpet.
Human bones by their everyday names.Lazybones: Lazybones is a nickname for an idle person, and it's a word, not an actual bone.
Human bones by their everyday names.Herringbone: Herringbone is a zigzag pattern that looks like a fish skeleton, so it's named for a fish bone, not a human one.
Human bones by their everyday names.Bone china: Bone china is a fine porcelain made with ground animal bone ash, which gives it translucency and strength.
Human bones by their everyday names.Bonfire: Bonfire comes from 'bone fire', because medieval fires burned bones, but it's not a bone.
Human bones by their everyday names.Bonehead: A bonehead is a stupid person, and it's slang, not a bone.
Human bones by their everyday names.Bone dry: Bone dry means completely dry, and it is a figure of speech, not a body part.
Human bones by their everyday names.Bonbon: A bonbon is a sweet from the French word for good, and it has no relation to bones despite 'bon'.
Human bones by their everyday names.Jawbreaker: A jawbreaker is a hard candy so large it seems to endanger your jaw, but it's not a bone.

Things a pirate owns.Eye patch: Some think pirates wore eye patches to keep one eye adapted to darkness for fighting below deck, though that's a theory, not proven.
Things a pirate owns.Parrot: The parrot-on-shoulder image comes largely from Treasure Island's Long John Silver and his parrot, Captain Flint.
Things a pirate owns.Treasure map: Real pirates almost never buried treasure on marked islands; the X marks the spot idea comes mostly from fiction.
Things a pirate owns.Cutlass: The short, curved cutlass suited cramped ships, where a long sword would snag on rigging and low ceilings.
Things a pirate owns.Peg leg: A sailor who lost a leg could often keep working at sea, and wooden peg legs were real replacement limbs.
Things a pirate owns.Spyglass: A spyglass was a collapsible telescope, letting sailors spot sails on the horizon miles away.
Things a pirate owns.Ship: Pirate ships were often captured merchant vessels, and pirates frequently favored fast, small boats.
Things a pirate owns.Cannon: Pirates often used cannons more as a threat than a weapon; they preferred scaring ships into surrender without a fight.
Things a pirate owns.Tricorn hat: The three-cornered hat was common 1700s fashion, not pirate-specific, and sailors and gentlemen wore it too.
Things a pirate owns.Jolly Roger: The skull-and-crossbones flag was a warning, and pirates often raised it to scare a ship into surrender.
Things a pirate owns.Rum barrel: Rum and grog were common at sea because fresh water spoiled quickly in wooden barrels.
Things a pirate owns.Hook hand: Hook hands are mostly fiction, made famous by Captain Hook in Peter Pan; real pirates rarely had hooks for hands.
Things a pirate owns.Compass: Compass needles point north because Earth acts as a giant magnet, and ship captains relied on them in open water.
Things a pirate owns.Spacesuit: Spacesuits date from the 20th century, long after the Golden Age of Piracy in the early 1700s.
Things a pirate owns.Laptop: Laptops arrived centuries after pirate days; the golden age of piracy ended around the 1720s.
Things a pirate owns.Skateboard: Skateboards appeared in California in the 1950s, more than two centuries after Blackbeard.
Things a pirate owns.Lightsaber: The lightsaber is from Star Wars in 1977, while the Golden Age of Piracy ended in the 1720s.
Things a pirate owns.Smartphone: Pirates navigated by stars and compasses, and the first smartphones didn't arrive until the 1990s.
Things a pirate owns.Tiara: Women like Anne Bonny and Mary Read were real pirates, but they wore ordinary clothes, not tiaras.
Things a pirate owns.Snowmobile: Pirates sailed warm waters like the Caribbean, and the snowmobile wasn't invented until the 20th century.
Things a pirate owns.Hairdryer: Pirates had no electricity, and the handheld hair dryer wasn't invented until the early 20th century.
Things a pirate owns.Briefcase: A briefcase is a modern business item; pirates carried their loot in chests.
Things a pirate owns.Lawnmower: The lawnmower was invented in 1830 by Edwin Budding in England, well after the pirate era.
Things a pirate owns.Selfie stick: The selfie stick is a 21st-century gadget; a pirate captain's portrait would have been painted.

Things a caveman would have.Club: A club is the classic caveman weapon, and real prehistoric wooden clubs rarely survive, as wood rots in most soils.
Things a caveman would have.Spear: Wooden spears are real: the Schoningen spears from Germany are about 300,000 years old and are among the oldest hunting weapons known.
Things a caveman would have.Fire: Fire is the great caveman tool, and evidence of controlled fire among early humans goes back at least about a million years.
Things a caveman would have.Animal skin: Animal skins kept early humans warm, and bone needles let them sew hides into tailored clothing for ice-age cold.
Things a caveman would have.Stone axe: A stone axe is a core prehistoric tool, and hand axes were made for over a million years by early humans.
Things a caveman would have.Cave painting: Cave paintings, as in Lascaux in France, are often over 17,000 years old, and some in Indonesia are over 40,000.
Things a caveman would have.Flint: Flint is a hard stone that breaks to a sharp edge, and striking it against pyrite makes sparks for fire.
Things a caveman would have.Bone needle: Bone needles with an eye hole date back about 40,000 years, and they were key to sewing ice-age fur clothes.
Things a caveman would have.Torch: A torch lit caves for painters and hunters, and fire-lit lamps of animal fat date back some 40,000 years.
Things a caveman would have.Smartphone: A smartphone is some 50,000 years too late for any caveman, and its screen is brighter than a cave's flickering torch.
Things a caveman would have.Wristwatch: A wristwatch is a modern timepiece, and cavemen told time with the sun and seasons.
Things a caveman would have.Microwave: A microwave needs electricity, which no caveman had, and he warmed his meal over a fire instead.
Things a caveman would have.Car: The car arrived in the 1880s, and cavemen's fastest transport was their own legs or a lucky river current.
Things a caveman would have.Toaster: A toaster needs electricity, and early humans toasted food by simply holding it over flames.
Things a caveman would have.Television: A television is far out of time, and a caveman's screen was a campfire he gazed into after dark.
Things a caveman would have.Laptop: A laptop is a modern invention, and cave dwellers stored their stories in painting and oral tradition.
Things a caveman would have.Plastic bottle: A plastic bottle is a modern creation, since plastic wasn't even invented until the 1800s, and the bottle came later.
Things a caveman would have.Zipper: A zipper was only invented in the 1890s and perfected in the early 1900s, so cavemen used ties and bone toggles.
Things a caveman would have.Light bulb: The light bulb was perfected around 1879 by Edison and others, long after cave dwellers' firelight.
Things a caveman would have.Bicycle: A bicycle is only about 200 years old, so a caveman would have no wheels at all, as the wheel came about 5,500 years ago.
Things a caveman would have.Sunglasses: Sunglasses are not a cavemen item, though Inuit people made snow goggles from bone or wood to cut glare for thousands of years.
Things a caveman would have.Paper clip: A paper clip is modern, since paper itself came from China about 2,000 years ago and paper clips in the 1800s.
Things a caveman would have.Credit card: A credit card arrived in the 1950s, and early humans traded by barter or shells instead.
Things a caveman would have.Electric guitar: An electric guitar is a 20th-century invention, but bone flutes from over 40,000 years ago show music is truly ancient.

Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Spider: Spiders in a bed are rarer than you'd think: most of them prefer corners and webs, not warm humans.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Snake: Snakes love warm places, and a bed has plenty of body heat, which is why they sometimes turn up where they shouldn't.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Crumbs: Crumbs in bed are more irritating than harmful, and you can feel them because skin is sensitive to tiny pokes.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Sand: Sand finds its way into everything after the beach, and it can scratch like fine sandpaper between the sheets.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Wet towel: A wet towel left in bed means a damp, chilly mess, and a moist mattress can also grow mold.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Scorpion: Scorpions can survive without food for months, and they glow blue-green under ultraviolet light.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Frog: A frog in the bed is a classic prank; many species can leap many times their body length.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Lego brick: Stepping on a Lego brick is notoriously painful; finding one in bed is just as bad.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Bedbugs: Bedbugs feed on blood, hide in mattress seams, and can live for months without a meal.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Cactus: Cactus spines are barbed and painful, and the plant stores water in its fleshy stem, so it can survive months of drought.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Mud: Mud in bed means dirty sheets and a long laundry day, and a muddy mattress is harder to clean than most.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Cold spaghetti: Cold spaghetti in bed is simply gross, and an unforgettable prank for any sleeper.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Pillow: A good pillow matters, since most people spend about a third of their lives asleep, and a decent one supports the neck.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Duvet: A duvet comes from the French word for down, and a warm one traps air between its fibers for insulation.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Teddy bear: A teddy bear is named for Theodore Roosevelt, who refused to shoot a tethered bear on a 1902 hunting trip.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Blanket: A blanket is among the oldest bedding items, and the word comes from the French for white wool.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Clean sheets: Clean sheets are a famous small pleasure, and surveys keep naming them among people's favorite little luxuries.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Hot water bottle: A hot water bottle dates back to the 1800s and is still a cozy, cheap way to warm a bed.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Pajamas: Pajamas come from the Hindi and Urdu word for loose trousers, and British colonists brought them home from India.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Bolster: A bolster is a long cylindrical pillow, common in India and Europe, and it supports the neck or back.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Electric blanket: Electric blankets began in the early 1900s, and modern ones have safety controls and timers.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Throw pillow: A throw pillow is decorative and can add comfort, and it's a pleasant addition to a bed.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Quilt: A quilt is stitched layers of fabric and batting, and quilting traditions stretch back centuries across many cultures.
Things you'd hate to find in your bed.Mattress topper: A mattress topper adds a layer of cushioning, and it's a way to refresh a worn mattress.

Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Sacked: Sacked is a British word; the origin is probably from workers being handed their tools in a sack when dismissed.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Dismissed: Dismissed is the formal word, and it's used in many contracts and legal documents to mean an employer ended the job.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Let go: Let go is a polite euphemism, often used when a layoff isn't about a person's performance.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Axed: Axed is the idea of chopping something off, and it's often used for cutting jobs or even entire TV shows.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Canned: Canned is American slang, possibly from the old idea of being thrown out like trash, and has been used since the 1900s.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Terminated: Terminated is the formal word, and in some sources it is used in contracts to mean an agreement ending.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Given the boot: The phrase refers to being kicked out, and a boot as a symbol of dismissal goes back to at least the 1800s.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Shown the door: Shown the door is a polite way of being escorted out, usually after a firm conversation.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Booted: Booted comes from the same kicking image as "given the boot," and is also used for being thrown out of a team or a party.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Discharged: Discharged is used for dismissals from the military, and the phrase "dishonorable discharge" can follow someone for life.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Promoted: A promotion is the opposite of a firing, and means moving up the ranks with better pay.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Hired: To be hired is to start a job, so it's the opposite of being fired.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Retired: Retiring is leaving work by choice, usually at an older age, so there is no blame involved.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Resigned: Resigning is quitting on your own, and the difference matters because the person might qualify for different benefits.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Quit: You quit by choice, so this is your own decision, not an employer's.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Transferred: A transfer moves you to another post, and you keep your job, so it isn't a dismissal.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Recruited: Being recruited means someone sought you out for a job, which is the very opposite of dismissal.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Head-hunted: Head-hunting is when a specialist firm lures you away to a new role, and it's flattering rather than firing.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Onboarded: Onboarding is the process of welcoming a new hire, so the exact opposite of a send-off.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Tenured: Tenure gives academics long-term job protection, making them especially hard to fire.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Employed: To be employed is to have a job, so it's the state firing takes you out of.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Reinstated: Reinstated means given your job back, and sometimes happens after an unfair dismissal is overturned.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Rehired: Rehired means being taken on again, and some bosses hire back the very person they let go.
Ways to say 'fired from a job'.Interviewed: An interview comes before a job, not at its end, so it doesn't mean being fired.

Things a gardener uses.Trowel: A trowel is a small hand shovel used for planting bulbs and seedlings, and its name comes from the Latin for a ladle.
Things a gardener uses.Rake: Rakes gather leaves or level soil, and the lawn rake's flexible tines are designed not to damage grass.
Things a gardener uses.Hoe: Hoes weed the soil by cutting roots just under the surface, and the tool is one of the oldest farming implements.
Things a gardener uses.Watering can: Watering at the roots, ideally in the morning, helps plants, as wet leaves at night can encourage disease.
Things a gardener uses.Pruning shears: Clean cuts just above a bud encourage healthy regrowth, which is why pruners should be kept sharp.
Things a gardener uses.Wheelbarrow: The wheelbarrow dates to ancient China, where it was invented about 2,000 years ago.
Things a gardener uses.Garden hose: Garden hoses used to be made of rubber and leather, and modern ones come in vinyl.
Things a gardener uses.Spade: A spade has a flat blade for cutting and edging, and digging with it gives a clean slice.
Things a gardener uses.Leaf blower: Leaf blowers were invented in Japan in the 1970s, and some towns now restrict them over noise.
Things a gardener uses.Compost: Compost turns scraps into rich soil, and it's often called black gold by gardeners.
Things a gardener uses.Garden fork: A garden fork loosens compacted soil, and it breaks it up without slicing worms in half.
Things a gardener uses.Seed packets: A seed can stay alive for years, and some old seeds have even sprouted after centuries.
Things a gardener uses.Kneeling pad: A kneeling pad saves knees on long weeding sessions and is an unglamorous but loved item.
Things a gardener uses.Whisk: A whisk beats eggs and cream in a kitchen, and it is no help to a gardener.
Things a gardener uses.Ladle: A ladle serves soup from a pot, and a gardener's nearest tool is a watering can with a long spout.
Things a gardener uses.Stethoscope: A stethoscope is a doctor's tool for hearing heartbeats, though plants have no heart to listen to.
Things a gardener uses.Easel: An easel holds a painter's canvas; plenty of painters set theirs up in gardens, as Monet did at Giverny.
Things a gardener uses.Anvil: Anvils belong to blacksmiths, and a gardener would never lift one, since a typical anvil weighs far more than a spade.
Things a gardener uses.Stapler: A stapler joins paper in an office, and a gardener's nearest binder is twine for tying up tall plants.
Things a gardener uses.Gavel: A gavel is a small mallet for judges and auctioneers, and a gardener's mallet is used on tent pegs or stakes.
Things a gardener uses.Plunger: A plunger clears blocked drains, which is a plumber's job rather than a gardener's.
Things a gardener uses.Thimble: A thimble guards a sewing finger, though foxglove flowers are named for fitting a fingertip like one.
Things a gardener uses.Colander: A colander drains pasta and rinses vegetables in the kitchen, so it's where the garden harvest ends up.
Things a gardener uses.Microscope: A microscope magnifies tiny things in a lab, though botanists use them to study plant cells.

Things a sculptor uses.Chisel: Michelangelo reportedly saw the figure already inside the stone and chiselled away whatever hid it.
Things a sculptor uses.Mallet: Sculptors strike chisels with wooden or rubber mallets rather than hammers because they spread the force and protect the tool.
Things a sculptor uses.Clay: Sculptors often build a small clay model, called a maquette, before casting or carving the final piece.
Things a sculptor uses.Marble: Carrara marble from Italy supplied Michelangelo's David and still supplies sculptors worldwide.
Things a sculptor uses.Rasp: A coarse file for shaping stone and plaster, smoothing what the chisel leaves behind.
Things a sculptor uses.Loop tool: A wire loop on a handle scoops clay away, used to hollow out sculptures so they don't crack in the kiln.
Things a sculptor uses.Armature: A skeleton of wire or metal inside a clay sculpture keeps the soft material from collapsing.
Things a sculptor uses.Bronze: Bronze sculpture is cast using the lost-wax process, and the Greek Riace Warriors from about 450 BCE are among the finest.
Things a sculptor uses.Plaster: Plaster of Paris is used for moulds and casts, and is named for the gypsum deposits near Montmartre.
Things a sculptor uses.Calipers: Used to measure and transfer proportions from model to stone, as in the pointing method.
Things a sculptor uses.Riffler: A small curved rasp bent to reach tight spots on stone, wood and metal.
Things a sculptor uses.Stethoscope: A doctor's listening tool, with nothing to shape in a studio.
Things a sculptor uses.Whisk: A cook's tool, not for shaping stone or clay.
Things a sculptor uses.Ladle: Foundry workers pour molten bronze from a big ladle, which makes this the cleverest near miss.
Things a sculptor uses.Plunger: A plumber's tool for blocked drains, nothing to do with the studio.
Things a sculptor uses.Thimble: A seamstress's fingertip guard, not a sculptor's tool.
Things a sculptor uses.Fishing rod: An angler's rod, with no use in carving or casting.
Things a sculptor uses.Gavel: A judge's mallet; a sculptor's mallet is similar but strikes chisels.
Things a sculptor uses.Saddle: A horse's seat, not a sculptor's tool; though an equestrian statue shows one in bronze.
Things a sculptor uses.Sextant: A navigator's tool for measuring the sun's angle, while sculptors take measures with calipers.
Things a sculptor uses.Stapler: Joins sheets of paper, and is no help in the studio.
Things a sculptor uses.Piping bag: A baker's icing tool, though sculptors of sugar and chocolate may use something like it.
Things a sculptor uses.Lasso: A cowboy's looped rope with no place in the sculpture studio.
Things a sculptor uses.Megaphone: Amplifies the voice; sculpture is silent work, apart from the clatter of the mallet.

Things a chef wears.Toque: Said to have 100 pleats, symbolising the ways a chef can cook an egg, and popularised by Marie-Antoine Carême.
Things a chef wears.Chef's jacket: Traditionally white and double-breasted, so it can be reversed to hide stains, and its thick fabric insulates against heat.
Things a chef wears.Apron: An apron shields clothes and legs from spills and hot splashes, and chefs wear it long.
Things a chef wears.Neckerchief: Originally worn to wipe sweat and keep it from dripping into food, and to shield the neck from heat.
Things a chef wears.Checked trousers: The black-and-white check hides spills and stains.
Things a chef wears.Kitchen clogs: Slip-resistant, closed-toe shoes protect from spills and dropped knives.
Things a chef wears.Side towel: Tucked into the apron string to grab hot pans; a wet one conducts heat dangerously.
Things a chef wears.Skull cap: A close-fitting cap used in busy kitchens in place of the tall toque, keeping hair out of food.
Things a chef wears.Hairnet: Required by food-safety rules in many places, it keeps hair away from plates.
Things a chef wears.Hard hat: Construction wear; a kitchen rarely has falling objects overhead.
Things a chef wears.Hi-vis vest: Worn by road crews so traffic can see them, which a kitchen doesn't need.
Things a chef wears.Spurs: Cowboy footwear worn to nudge a horse, not in the kitchen.
Things a chef wears.Chaps: Leather leg guards for riders and loggers, not chefs.
Things a chef wears.Turnout coat: A firefighter's heavy coat, with layers that shield from heat far beyond what a chef's jacket does.
Things a chef wears.Waders: Waterproof trousers for fishing, and not for the kitchen.
Things a chef wears.Lab coat: White like a chef's jacket but worn by scientists; food-lab chefs do sometimes wear one.
Things a chef wears.Stethoscope: René Laennec's 1816 invention hangs round a doctor's neck; chefs wear a side towel there instead, ready for hot pans.
Things a chef wears.Kevlar vest: Body armour for police, not for the kitchen.
Things a chef wears.Tool belt: Carpenters and electricians wear them, but chefs keep knives in a roll or block.
Things a chef wears.Tiara: A crown for royals and beauty queens, and not for the kitchen.
Things a chef wears.Judge's wig: UK judges still wear horsehair wigs in court, as a ceremonial tradition, not in a kitchen.
Things a chef wears.Bearskin: The tall fur caps of the British Foot Guards at Buckingham Palace rival a toque in height.
Things a chef wears.Swim cap: A swimmer's cap, not a chef's, though a chef's skull cap looks similar.
Things a chef wears.Welding mask: Protects a welder's eyes from the arc, not from kitchen steam.

Originally written in German.The Metamorphosis: Kafka wrote this about a salesman who wakes as a giant insect; it was published in 1915, and he asked friends to burn his work.
Originally written in German.The Trial: Kafka's unfinished novel opens with Josef K. arrested for a crime he is never told about; the word 'Kafkaesque' comes from this style.
Originally written in German.Faust: Goethe spent about 60 years on this drama of a scholar who bargains with the devil, and it is a central work of German literature.
Originally written in German.Siddhartha: Hesse's 1922 novel follows a young Brahmin's quest for enlightenment in ancient India, and was beloved by the 1960s counterculture.
Originally written in German.Steppenwolf: Hesse's 1927 novel about a loner torn between man and wolf became a counterculture cult classic, and the rock band is named after it.
Originally written in German.The Magic Mountain: Thomas Mann's 1924 novel set in a Swiss sanatorium follows Hans Castorp, who visits for three weeks and stays for seven years.
Originally written in German.Heidi: Johanna Spyri's 1880 novel about a Swiss orphan girl and her grandfather was written in German.
Originally written in German.Bambi: Felix Salten's 1923 novel about a deer in the forest was originally written in German; Disney made it famous.
Originally written in German.Perfume: Patrick Süskind's 1985 novel about a man with an extraordinary sense of smell became a worldwide bestseller; set in 1700s France.
Originally written in German.The Tin Drum: Günter Grass's 1959 novel is narrated by a boy who stops growing at age three, and he used his drum to scream.
Originally written in German.The Reader: Bernhard Schlink's 1995 novel about a teenager's affair with an older woman was a rare German bestseller in America.
Originally written in German.Grimms' Fairy Tales: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm gathered these stories in 1812, first in German, and they were more grim than in later editions.
Originally written in German.Madame Bovary: Flaubert's novel is French, not German; it caused a scandal in the 1850s.
Originally written in German.Candide: Voltaire's French satire, written in 1759, ends with the line about cultivating one's garden.
Originally written in German.Don Quixote: Cervantes wrote this Spanish epic about a knight who battles windmills.
Originally written in German.Pinocchio: Collodi wrote it in Italian; the puppet's nose grows when he lies.
Originally written in German.The Little Prince: Saint-Exupéry wrote this French fable, in which a prince visits planets.
Originally written in German.War and Peace: Tolstoy wrote this novel in Russian, not German.
Originally written in German.Pippi Longstocking: Astrid Lindgren wrote this in Swedish, and her heroine can lift a horse.
Originally written in German.The Ugly Duckling: Andersen wrote this in Danish, about a swan raised by ducks.
Originally written in German.The Stranger: Camus's novel was written in French, and its title in French is L'Étranger.
Originally written in German.The Divine Comedy: Dante wrote it in Italian, in the early 1300s.
Originally written in German.Peter Pan: J. M. Barrie wrote this play in English, about a boy who won't grow up.
Originally written in German.Dracula: Bram Stoker's 1897 novel is English (Irish author), told through letters and diary entries.

Ancient Greek tragedies.Oedipus Rex: Sophocles' tragedy in which Oedipus unknowingly killed his father and married his mother; Freud borrowed the name.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Antigone: Sophocles' heroine defies King Creon to bury her brother, putting divine law over state law.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Medea: Euripides' 431 BC tragedy about a woman who takes terrible revenge on her husband; it placed only third at its first staging.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Electra: Both Sophocles and Euripides wrote versions about the daughter who plots revenge for her father's murder.
Ancient Greek tragedies.The Bacchae: Euripides' late tragedy, performed after his death, in which Dionysus' followers tear King Pentheus apart.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Agamemnon: The first part of Aeschylus' Oresteia, the only complete ancient Greek tragic trilogy that survives; Clytemnestra kills her husband.
Ancient Greek tragedies.The Trojan Women: Euripides, 415 BC, shows the women of Troy after its fall; it is often read as anti-war, soon after Athens' brutal Melos campaign.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Prometheus Bound: Attributed to Aeschylus, though scholars debate it, about the Titan chained to a rock for giving fire to humans.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Hippolytus: Euripides' tale of Phaedra's forbidden love for her stepson; his second version won first prize in 428 BC.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Ajax: Sophocles' play in which a hero, driven mad, slaughters sheep thinking they are his enemies, then kills himself.
Ancient Greek tragedies.The Persians: Aeschylus' 472 BC drama of Persia's defeat at Salamis, from the Persian side; it is the oldest surviving Greek play.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Lysistrata: An Aristophanes comedy in which women go on a sex strike to end the war; comic, not tragic.
Ancient Greek tragedies.The Frogs: An Aristophanes comedy in which Dionysus goes to Hades to bring back a dead poet, and Aeschylus and Euripides compete.
Ancient Greek tragedies.The Clouds: An Aristophanes comedy that mocks Socrates, who is shown hanging in a basket; it is a comedy, not a tragedy.
Ancient Greek tragedies.The Birds: An Aristophanes comedy in which two Athenians found a city in the sky, source of 'Cloud Cuckoo Land'.
Ancient Greek tragedies.The Wasps: An Aristophanes comedy about an old man obsessed with jury duty, so a comedy rather than a tragedy.
Ancient Greek tragedies.The Iliad: Homer's epic poem about the Trojan War: an epic, not a play, though many Greek tragedies borrowed from its stories.
Ancient Greek tragedies.The Odyssey: Homer's epic of Odysseus's long journey home, a poem and not a drama, though tragedians drew on its stories.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Hamlet: A Shakespeare tragedy: tragic in tone, but Danish in setting and English in origin, written some 2,000 years after the Greeks.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Phèdre: Racine's 1677 French tragedy that retells the Greek Hippolytus myth, so close but not ancient.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Faust: Goethe's German drama about a scholar's bargain with the devil; a tragedy, but from the 19th century and not Greek.
Ancient Greek tragedies.The Aeneid: Virgil's Roman epic poem, reportedly left unfinished, with Virgil wanting it burned; not Greek tragedy.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Doctor Faustus: Christopher Marlowe's Elizabethan tragedy of a scholar selling his soul; English, not Greek.
Ancient Greek tragedies.Tartuffe: Molière's comedy of a pious fraud, banned for years under Church pressure; French and comic, not Greek and tragic.

Things shaped like a cylinder.Soup can: Canning was invented in the early 1800s for Napoleon's army, years before the can opener was, so early cans were cut open with chisels.
Things shaped like a cylinder.AA battery: A standard alkaline AA delivers about 1.5 volts, and the same size is used worldwide, so a cell from any brand fits.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Pipe: A round cross-section carries fluid under pressure most evenly, which is why water pipes are cylindrical, as in Roman lead pipes called fistulae.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Drum: A drum is a hollow cylinder with a stretched skin on one or both ends, and the oldest known examples are over 6,000 years old.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Toilet paper roll: Cardboard tubes from toilet paper became a craft staple, and the perforated roll was patented in the US by Seth Wheeler in the 1880s.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Pringles can: Its designer, Fredric Baur, was so proud that when he died in 2008 some of his ashes were reportedly buried in a Pringles can.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Rolling pin: A rolling pin works as a cylinder because it presses evenly across the dough as it rolls, and some bakers prefer French ones with no handles.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Paint can: Paint cans are cylindrical, as that shape resists pressure, and the lip around the lid is designed to take a screwdriver.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Glue stick: The glue stick was invented in Germany around 1969 by Henkel, and was inspired by a lipstick-like tube.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Chapstick: Lip balm's stick shape comes from the tube design, and the brand began in the 1880s in Lynchburg, Virginia, as a hand-rolled wax stick.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Drinking straw: The first straws were made from natural rye grass, and the paper straw patent was granted to Marvin Stone in 1888.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Hockey puck: Regulation pucks are vulcanized rubber, one inch thick and three inches in diameter, and they are frozen before games so they bounce less.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Ice cream cone: It's a cone, not a cylinder, and one popular story says it began at the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis when a waffle was rolled up.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Pyramid: A pyramid has a square base and four triangular sides rising to a point, and the Great Pyramid was the tallest man-made structure for about 3,800 years.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Basketball: Spheres have no flat faces or edges at all, so a basketball counts as neither a cylinder nor a cone, and it's about 24 cm across.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Dice: A cube has six flat square faces, so it fails here, since a cylinder has two round ends and one curved side.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Book: A book is a rectangular block, though a scroll, its ancient predecessor, would be a cylinder when rolled up.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Brick: A brick is a rectangular block, which is a shape that allows stacking without gaps, and a standard one is about 8 by 4 by 2.5 inches.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Egg: The egg is an ovoid, a rounded shape stronger than a cylinder at resisting pressure from the outside, as every chicken knows.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Traffic cone: The traffic cone was invented by Charles Scanlon in 1940, who worked in street painting in Los Angeles.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Party hat: A party hat is a cone with a point on top, not a cylinder, though it is rolled from a flat piece of paper.
Things shaped like a cylinder.American football: The football is a prolate spheroid, and its pointed ends let it spiral through the air when thrown.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Shoebox: A shoebox is a rectangular box with a lid, which is a rectangular prism and not a cylinder.
Things shaped like a cylinder.Banana: Bananas curve as they grow, because the fruit bends upward against gravity, a trait called negative geotropism.

Things shaped like a flat disc.Coin: Most coins have ridged or reeded edges, a trick dating back to when thieves shaved precious metal off smooth ones.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Pizza: Classic Neapolitan pizza is protected by tradition: the dough must be stretched by hand, never rolled with a pin.
Things shaped like a flat disc.CD: A compact disc stores data as microscopic pits along one continuous spiral track that would stretch for miles if unwound.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Frisbee: The Frisbee began as a pie tin: students tossed empty Frisbie Baking Company pans, inspiring the toy's name.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Pancake: Pancakes are among the oldest foods, and a pancake race has been run in Olney, England, since the 15th century.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Dinner plate: Plates have grown: the average dinner plate is noticeably larger today than a century ago, nudging people toward bigger portions.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Hockey puck: A regulation puck is made of vulcanized rubber and is frozen before games so it slides rather than bounces.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Tortilla: In Spain a tortilla is an egg and potato omelet, while in Mexico it is the flat corn or wheat bread.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Vinyl record: A record's sound is a single groove wiggling in a spiral, and the needle follows its wiggles to recreate the music.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Manhole cover: Manhole covers are round because a round lid can't fall through its own hole, whatever way it's turned.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Poker chip: Casino chips often hold hidden security features like embedded RFID tags, and are usually clay composite or plastic.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Coaster: Coasters trace to beer mats in Europe, where they started as thick pulp discs to stop drinks marking tables.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Cookie: The word cookie comes from Dutch koekje, meaning little cake, and the first ones were test bakes of cake batter.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Basketball: A basketball is a sphere, not a disc, and its pebbled surface helps with grip and dribbling control.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Egg: An egg is an oval shape, deliberately lopsided: one end is narrower, so an egg rolls in a circle rather than straight off.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Book: A book is a rectangular block, and the standard paper sizes it uses come from ratios designed so halves keep the same shape.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Brick: A brick is a rectangular block, and a classic proportion lets you lay it with one hand while the other holds the mortar.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Dice: Dice are cubes, and on a standard die opposite faces always add up to seven.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Banana: A banana is curved and elongated, not flat, because the fruit grows upward against gravity, bending toward the sun.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Orange: An orange is a sphere, and its flat-topped cousin the mandarin is closer but still not truly a disc.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Marble: Marbles are tiny perfect spheres, and glass ones have been made in Germany and elsewhere since at least the 1800s.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Pyramid: A pyramid is a cone-like solid with a base and rising sides, so it is far from a flat disc; Giza's is about 140 meters tall.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Envelope: An envelope is a flat rectangle, not a disc, and the gummed flap was only popularized with 19th-century mass mailing.
Things shaped like a flat disc.Domino: A domino is a flat rectangular tile, with its two halves marked by pips, so it is flat but not disc-shaped.

Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Egg: The egg is the standard oval, and one end is narrower, which makes it roll in a circle instead of off a surface.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Rugby ball: Rugby balls were originally made from pig bladders, which is why they ended up oval instead of round.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.American football: The football's pointed oval shape is a prolate spheroid, which spins stably when thrown as a spiral.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Kiwi fruit: Kiwi fruit were once called Chinese gooseberries, and they were renamed in New Zealand in the 1950s for export.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Olive: Olive trees can live for well over a thousand years, and some in the Mediterranean are thought to be much older.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Jellybean: Jellybeans take their name from the bean-like shape and their soft, jelly-like center, and they took up to a week to make.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Easter egg: Egg decorating for spring celebrations goes back centuries, and eggs symbolized new life in many traditions.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Almond: The almond is a seed, not a true nut, and it's the pit of a fruit related to peaches.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Tic Tac: Tic Tacs are tiny oval mints, and the name comes from the sound the candy makes in the box.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Coffee bean: The coffee bean is a seed from a berry-like cherry, and most cherries hold two seeds with flat sides facing each other.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Basketball: A basketball is a sphere, and its pebbled surface is what makes dribbling and gripping possible.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Marble: Marbles are perfectly round glass balls, and the oldest ones date to ancient Egypt and Rome.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Dice: Standard dice are cubes, and the opposite faces always add up to seven.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Coin: Coins are flat discs, round in outline, and ridged edges once discouraged people from shaving off precious metal.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Pyramid: A pyramid has a square base and triangular sides, and the Great Pyramid was the tallest man-made structure for about 3,800 years.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Brick: A standard brick is a rectangular block, sized so that a builder can grip and lay it with one hand.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Book: A book is a rectangle, and the golden ratio is sometimes used to set page proportions.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Pizza box: A pizza box is a square, and the little plastic table in the middle keeps the lid off the cheese.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Sugar cube: Sugar cubes were invented in the 1840s by Jakub Kryštof Rad, after his wife cut her finger on a sugar loaf.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Banana: A banana is curved and elongated, not oval; its curve comes from the fruit growing upward toward the sun.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Pencil: Pencils are long cylinders, and the cores contain graphite, not lead.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Starfish: Starfish are star-shaped, and they can regrow lost arms, though they are not true fish.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Yield sign: A yield sign is a downward-pointing triangle, and it's one of the few road signs of this shape.
Things that are oval or egg-shaped.Orange: Oranges are close to round, and the color orange was named for the fruit, not the other way around.

Landmarks in New York City.Statue of Liberty: A gift from France in 1886, it was shipped in 350 pieces, and its green color is from copper reacting with air, a natural patina.
Landmarks in New York City.Chrysler Building: This Art Deco spire topped by stainless-steel arches was briefly the tallest building in the world in 1930, before the Empire State Building.
Landmarks in New York City.Central Park: It's a designed landscape, not a wild one, laid out by Olmsted and Vaux in the 1850s, and it covers about 843 acres.
Landmarks in New York City.Times Square: It was renamed for The New York Times, which moved there in 1904, and the New Year's Eve ball drop began in 1907.
Landmarks in New York City.Brooklyn Bridge: Opened in 1883, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world, and 21 elephants crossed it in 1884 to prove it safe.
Landmarks in New York City.Rockefeller Center: A group of 14 Art Deco buildings, it hosts the giant Christmas tree and an ice rink each winter.
Landmarks in New York City.Wall Street: Named for a wall built by Dutch settlers in the 1600s, this narrow street is shorthand for the American financial industry.
Landmarks in New York City.Grand Central: The terminal's main concourse has a ceiling mural of constellations, painted reversed, as seen from outside the sky.
Landmarks in New York City.Flatiron Building: This triangular skyscraper from 1902 gets its name from its shape, which looks like a cast-iron clothes iron.
Landmarks in New York City.The High Line: This elevated park runs along an old freight rail line above Manhattan streets, and it opened in 2009 after being nearly demolished.
Landmarks in New York City.Coney Island: Brooklyn's seaside amusement area has the Cyclone coaster from 1927 and hosts the Nathan's hot dog eating contest each July 4th.
Landmarks in New York City.Yankee Stadium: The Bronx home of baseball's Yankees, one of baseball's most successful teams, with 27 World Series titles.
Landmarks in New York City.Broadway: The street runs the length of Manhattan and beyond, and its theatres in Midtown give the name to American commercial theatre.
Landmarks in New York City.Golden Gate Bridge: This is San Francisco's, not New York's, and its signature color is called International Orange.
Landmarks in New York City.Hollywood Sign: The sign in LA once read 'Hollywoodland', an advertisement for a housing development, in 1923.
Landmarks in New York City.Space Needle: Built for Seattle's 1962 World's Fair, this tower rises over 180 metres, and nowhere near New York.
Landmarks in New York City.Alcatraz: A San Francisco Bay island prison that held Al Capone, so it's on the wrong coast.
Landmarks in New York City.Willis Tower: Chicago's Willis Tower was once the tallest building in the world, and it was formerly called the Sears Tower.
Landmarks in New York City.Gateway Arch: At 630 feet, St. Louis's stainless-steel arch is the tallest man-made monument in the US, and it's no New York sight.
Landmarks in New York City.Liberty Bell: Philadelphia's famous cracked bell is a symbol of independence, but it's not in New York.
Landmarks in New York City.White House: The US president's home is in Washington, DC, and was rebuilt after British troops burned it in 1814.
Landmarks in New York City.Lincoln Memorial: A Washington DC monument, and its statue shows Lincoln seated, in a temple with 36 columns for the states in his time.
Landmarks in New York City.Fenway Park: Boston's famed baseball park opened in 1912, and its left-field wall known as the Green Monster is 37 feet tall.
Landmarks in New York City.Las Vegas Strip: A stretch of Las Vegas Boulevard with casinos and hotels, in Nevada and thousands of miles from New York.

Famous sports stadiums.Wembley: The original Wembley's twin towers stood from 1923 to 2003, and the new stadium's arch is 133 meters high.
Famous sports stadiums.Maracanã: Maracanã in Rio held about 200,000 for the 1950 World Cup final, when Brazil lost to Uruguay on home turf.
Famous sports stadiums.Camp Nou: Barcelona's home is Europe's largest club stadium, with a capacity of nearly 100,000 when fully open.
Famous sports stadiums.Old Trafford: Manchester United's home is nicknamed the Theatre of Dreams, a phrase coined by Bobby Charlton.
Famous sports stadiums.Yankee Stadium: Babe Ruth's home earned the nickname 'The House That Ruth Built' when it opened in 1923.
Famous sports stadiums.Fenway Park: Boston's Fenway Park, opened 1912, is MLB's oldest ballpark and is famous for its 37-foot Green Monster wall.
Famous sports stadiums.Wrigley Field: Wrigley Field's ivy-covered outfield walls date to 1937, and the Cubs didn't install lights until 1988.
Famous sports stadiums.Anfield: Liverpool's home is known for its Kop stand and the singing of 'You'll Never Walk Alone'.
Famous sports stadiums.San Siro: San Siro in Milan is shared by AC Milan and Inter, and is formally named Giuseppe Meazza after an Inter star.
Famous sports stadiums.Santiago Bernabéu: Real Madrid's ground is named for its former president, and can close its roof to host concerts.
Famous sports stadiums.Allianz Arena: Bayern Munich's stadium glows red, blue or white, since its facade is made of 2,760 inflated panels.
Famous sports stadiums.Lord's: Lord's in London is the 'home of cricket', and its famous sloping pitch drops about 2.5 meters.
Famous sports stadiums.MCG: The Melbourne Cricket Ground holds about 100,000 and hosted the 1956 Olympics and a Boxing Day Test each year.
Famous sports stadiums.Royal Albert Hall: Royal Albert Hall in London is a concert venue, not a sports stadium, though it has hosted boxing and tennis.
Famous sports stadiums.Carnegie Hall: Carnegie Hall is a New York concert hall, and the old joke asks how to get there: 'practice'.

Famous sports stadiums.La Scala: Milan's La Scala is a famed opera house, and its season opens each year on 7 December.
Famous sports stadiums.Broadway: Broadway is a theater district in New York, and a street, not a stadium.

Famous sports stadiums.Abbey Road: Abbey Road is a London street with a recording studio and The Beatles' famous zebra crossing, not a stadium.
Famous sports stadiums.Kremlin: The Kremlin in Moscow is a fortified complex and the seat of the Russian government, not a sports ground.

Eye makeup.Mascara: The word comes from Spanish mascara, mask, and the first commercial one was cake form applied with a brush.
Eye makeup.Eyeliner: Ancient Egyptians lined their eyes with kohl, believed to protect against the evil eye and the sun's glare.
Eye makeup.Eyeshadow: Ancient Egyptians ground green malachite into eyeshadow, long before modern pigments.
Eye makeup.False eyelashes: First patented in 1911, and D. W. Griffith used them in his film Intolerance in 1916.
Eye makeup.Kohl: Ancient Egyptians made it from galena, and it may have protected eyes as well as decorated them.
Eye makeup.Brow pencil: Thin brows ruled in the 1930s, when Hollywood stars plucked and redrew theirs.
Eye makeup.Brow gel: Works like hair gel for eyebrows, keeping the hairs brushed and held in place.
Eye makeup.Lash primer: A pale base that primes lashes so mascara goes on thicker and lasts longer.
Eye makeup.Eyebrow pomade: A wax-based product used to define and fill brows, and often applied with a small brush.
Eye makeup.Lipstick: The first modern tube, a metal container with a push-up mechanism, appeared in 1915, and it's for lips, not eyes.
Eye makeup.Lip gloss: Gives lips shine from oils and wax rather than color, so it belongs to the lips, not the eyes.
Eye makeup.Blush: Colors the cheeks, not the eyes, and the older name for it was rouge.
Eye makeup.Bronzer: Adds warmth to cheeks and face, not eye color.
Eye makeup.Foundation: Makeup artist Max Factor created many film-era base products, and Pan-Cake arrived in 1937.
Eye makeup.Nail polish: Modern polish grew from car-paint technology in the 1920s, and it goes on nails, not eyes.
Eye makeup.Lip liner: Defines the edge of the lips, not the eyes.
Eye makeup.Rouge: French for red, used on cheeks and lips; the name appears in Moulin Rouge.
Eye makeup.Lip balm: ChapStick arrived in the 1880s, invented by Dr. Charles Browne Fleet, and it belongs to the lips.
Eye makeup.Perfume: Applied to skin and clothes, not the eyes, and the word comes from Latin per fumum, through smoke.
Eye makeup.Hairspray: Aerosol hairspray holds hair, and it belongs to hair care.
Eye makeup.Cuticle oil: Softens the skin around the nails, not the eyes.
Eye makeup.Deodorant: Antiperspirant stops sweat, while deodorant only tackles odor, and neither goes near the eyes.
Eye makeup.Lip stain: Tints lips with a long-lasting color, but it's lip, not eye, makeup.
Eye makeup.Hand cream: Moisturizes hands and nothing else, not related to the eyes.
